trials.eligibility:
Key Inclusion Criteria:

MAD Period

* Participants must have a diagnosis of ALS consistent with the Gold Coast criteria.
* No pathogenic variants, likely pathogenic variants, or variants of uncertain significance in the superoxide dismutase 1 (SOD1) or fused in sarcoma (FUS) genes (confirmed by central genetic testing).
* Greater than or equal to (≥) 50% of predicted value for slow vital capacity (SVC) as adjusted for sex, age, and height (from the sitting position).
* If taking riluzole, participant must be on a stable dose for ≥ 30 days prior to Day 1 and expected to remain at that dose until the final study visit end of study (EOS)/early termination (ET), unless the Investigator determines that it should be discontinued for medical reasons, in which case it may not be restarted during the study.

OLE

* Participants must have completed Study 303AS101 MAD period; all pre-dose assessments for the end of MAD treatment period visit (Day 113 for Cohorts A, B, C, and Day 169 for Cohort D) must be completed prior to dosing in OLE.

Key Exclusion Criteria:

MAD Period

* History or positive test result at screening for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). The requirement for testing at screening may be omitted if it is not permitted by local regulations.
* History of confounding neuromuscular or neurological disorder that is expected to have a progressive (i.e., worsening) course during the study, and/or is expected to be associated with elevations in NfL, in the opinion of the Investigator.
* Current or anticipated need, in the opinion of the Investigator, of a diaphragm pacing system during the study period.
* Requires permanent ventilation (using \> 22 hours per day \[h/day\] invasive or non-invasive ventilation)
* History of a deep venous thrombosis or pulmonary embolism ≤2 years of screening, or since the date of ALS diagnosis, whichever is longer.
* Treatment with an approved ALS disease-modifying therapy other than riluzole or edaravone, or another investigational drug (including investigational drugs for ALS through compassionate use programs), biological agent, or device within 1 month or 5 half-lives of study agent, whichever is longer, before completion of Screening.
* Current enrollment or a plan to enroll in any interventional clinical study. Participation in a noninterventional study focused on ALS natural history may be allowed at the discretion of the Investigator and after consultation with the Sponsor.

OLE

* Any new condition or worsening of an existing condition that, according to the Investigator, would make the participant unsuitable for inclusion, could interfere with the assessment of safety, or would compromise the ability of the participant to undergo study procedures.
* Clinically significant abnormalities (based on most recent assessments in MAD period) in hematology, blood chemistry parameters, or 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) prior to first OLE visit that would make the participant unsuitable for inclusion as assessed by the Investigator.

Note: Other protocol-defined Inclusion/Exclusion criteria do apply.

trials.title: EDAS Revascularization for Symptomatic Intracranial Atherosclerotic Steno-occlusive Disease
trials.summary: ERSIAS IIb is a multicenter randomized controlled trial, with a Phase IIb design, to find out whether encephaloduroarteriosynangiosis (EDAS), a type of indirect surgical revascularization of the brain, added to intensive medical management, lowers the rate of recurrent stroke and death compared with intensive medical management alone. The trial enrolls 170 adults who have had a recent ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack caused by intracranial atherosclerotic disease, with a narrowing or blockage of at least 70% of the intracranial internal carotid artery or the middle cerebral artery and reduced blood flow in the territory of that artery. Participants are assigned at random, in equal numbers, to EDAS plus intensive medical management or to intensive medical management alone, and are followed for 18 to 54 months.

interventions.name: Encephaloduroarteriosynangiosis (EDAS)
interventions.description: EDAS is a form of indirect revascularization for cerebral arterial steno-occlusive disorders. The superficial temporal artery (STA) is dissected from the scalp, while maintaining its proximal and terminal connections to the external carotid artery and the skin tissues. The STA is then rerouted under the skull and placed in close proximity to the cortical branches of the middle cerebral artery without a direct anastomosis. EDAS is performed no later than 7 days after randomization.

interventions.name: Intensive medical management
interventions.description: Medical management administered to both study arms following current and updated standard-of-care parameters, with guidance and oversight from the trial's Medical Management Core. Antiplatelet treatment with aspirin for the entire follow-up and dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin plus a P2Y12 receptor inhibitor for up to 90 days after randomization; management of the primary risk factors targeting systolic blood pressure \<140 mmHg and LDL \<70 mg/dL; management of the secondary risk factors (diabetes, non-HDL cholesterol, smoking, weight, physical activity) with the assistance of a lifestyle modification program. The management protocol may be modified during the trial to reflect the most up-to-date, evidence-based practices; changes apply to participants in both groups.

arms.label: EDAS plus intensive medical management
arms.description: EDAS performed no later than 7 days after randomization, plus intensive medical management. Participants in this group receive aspirin without interruption and do not receive a P2Y12 inhibitor from 5 days before until 7 days after surgery.

arms.label: Intensive medical management alone
arms.description: Intensive medical management following current guidelines for the management of patients with symptomatic intracranial atherosclerotic disease.

primary_outcomes.measure: Rate of any stroke or death within 30 days of randomization, or ischemic stroke in the territory of the qualifying artery thereafter
primary_outcomes.description: The composite of any stroke (ischemic or hemorrhagic) or death within 30 days of randomization plus recurrent ischemic stroke in the territory of the qualifying artery thereafter during full follow-up. Possible events are centrally adjudicated; the outcome measure is the centrally adjudicated, blinded event, not the site-determined event. Cumulative event rates in the two groups are compared by Kaplan-Meier estimates at 2.5 years.
primary_outcomes.timeFrame: From randomization through the end of follow-up (minimum 18 months, maximum 54 months, mean 30 months)

trials.eligibility:
Inclusion Criteria:

1. Borderzone or superficial territorial ischemic stroke, or cortical TIA, within 30 days before enrollment, attributed to 70% to 100% atherosclerotic stenosis/occlusion of the intracranial ICA or the MCA (M1 or dominant/co-dominant M2). The eligible borderzone strokes are cortical (external) borderzone infarcts, located between the anterior and middle cerebral artery territories or between the middle and posterior cerebral artery territories; internal borderzone infarcts are not included. A cortical TIA is defined as transient cortical dysfunction evidenced by either visual field defects, spatial neglect, disorder of language, memory, or orientation. The corresponding cerebral artery atherosclerosis may be diagnosed by CTA, contrast-enhanced MRI, or catheter angiography.
2. Evidence of perfusion impairment (minimum: TMax delay ≥ 6 sec, vol ≥ 5 cc) in CTP or perfusion MRI.
3. Functional status better than severely disabled (mRS score 0-3).
4. Age ≥18 years and ≤90 years. If the patient is 18 to 49 years of age, at least 1 of the following should be present:

   * Insulin-dependent diabetes for at least 15 years.
   * At least 2 of the following atherosclerotic risk factors: SBP ≥130 mmHg or on antihypertensive therapy; dyslipidemia (LDL \>130 mg/dL, HDL \<40 mg/dL, fasting triglycerides \>150 mg/dL, or on lipid-lowering therapy); smoking; non-insulin-dependent diabetes or insulin-dependent diabetes less than 15 years in duration; family history of any of the following: myocardial infarction, coronary artery bypass, coronary artery angioplasty or stenting, stroke, carotid endarterectomy or stenting, peripheral vascular surgery in parent or sibling who was \<55 years of age for men or \<65 years of age for women at the time of the event.
   * History of any of the following: myocardial infarction, coronary artery bypass, coronary angioplasty or stenting, carotid endarterectomy or stenting, or peripheral vascular surgery for atherosclerotic disease.
   * Any stenosis/occlusion 50% to 100% of an extracranial carotid or vertebral artery, another intracranial artery, subclavian artery, coronary artery, iliac or femoral artery, other lower or upper extremity artery, mesenteric artery, or renal artery that was documented by non-invasive vascular imaging or catheter angiography and is considered atherosclerotic.
   * Aortic arch atheroma documented by non-invasive vascular imaging or catheter angiography.
   * Any aortic aneurysm documented by non-invasive vascular imaging or catheter angiography that is considered atherosclerotic.
5. Negative pregnancy test in a female who has had any menses 18 months prior to enrollment.
6. Patient willing and able to return for all follow-up visits required by the protocol.
7. Patient is available by telephone.
8. Patient understands the purpose and requirements of the trial, can make himself/herself understood, and has provided informed consent.

Exclusion Criteria:

1. CT or MRI evidence of an isolated perforator stroke as qualifying event, defined by the Imaging Core based on established templates of cerebral vascular territories.
2. Angioplasty, stenting, or endarterectomy of an ipsilateral extracranial carotid artery within 90 days prior to enrollment or planned within 90 days following enrollment.
3. Stenting of the qualifying intracranial artery at any time, including a stent placed during an endovascular attempt for the qualifying event. Thrombectomy or angioplasty without stent placement is not an exclusion; eligibility is determined on imaging obtained after the procedure.
4. Intracranial tumor or intracranial vascular malformation.
5. TIAs of increased frequency, duration, or severity, or ischemic stroke within 7 days prior to enrollment.
6. Infarct with hemorrhagic transformation within 30 days prior to enrollment.
7. Infarct with hemorrhagic transformation of parenchymatous hematoma type-2 within 90 days prior to enrollment.
8. History of primary intracerebral (parenchymal) hemorrhage.
9. Any other intracranial hemorrhage (subarachnoid, subdural, epidural) within 90 days prior to enrollment.
10. Any untreated chronic subdural hematoma greater than 5 mm in thickness.
11. Intracranial stenosis due to non-atherosclerotic etiologies: evidence of arterial dissection; moyamoya disease; any known vasculitic disease; herpes zoster, varicella zoster or other viral vasculopathy; neurosyphilis; any other intracranial infection; any intracranial stenosis associated with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pleocytosis; radiation-induced vasculopathy; fibromuscular dysplasia; sickle cell disease; neurofibromatosis; reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome; postpartum angiopathy; suspected vasospastic process; suspected recanalized embolus.
12. Unequivocal cardiac sources of embolism as stroke etiology, including chronic or paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, symptomatic ventricular arrhythmias, severe or symptomatic aortic or mitral stenosis, mechanical valve, endocarditis, intracardiac clot or vegetation.
13. Myocardial infarction within 1 month prior to enrollment.
14. Unstable or severe angina.
15. Ejection fraction less than 40%.
16. Known allergy or contraindication to general anesthesia.
17. Known allergy to aspirin.
18. Known life-threatening allergy to contrast dye.
19. Active peptic ulcer disease, major systemic hemorrhage within 30 days, active bleeding diathesis, platelets \<100,000/mL, hematocrit \<30%, international normalized ratio \>1.5, clotting factor abnormality that increases the risk of bleeding.
20. Current alcohol or substance abuse within 1 month from enrollment.
21. Uncontrolled severe hypertension (SBP \>180 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure \>115 mmHg).
22. Severe liver impairment (AST or ALT \>3× normal, cirrhosis) that may prevent the use of statins.
23. Severe renal impairment (creatinine \>3.0 mg/dL or on dialysis).
24. Other major surgery planned in the next 90 days after enrollment that may require suspension of antiplatelet therapy.
25. Dementia or a psychiatric problem that prevents the patient from reliably following an outpatient program.
26. Co-morbid conditions that may limit survival to less than 3 years.
27. Pregnancy or of childbearing potential and unwilling to use contraception for the duration of the dual antiplatelet treatment period of the trial.
28. Active enrollment in another therapeutic trial that would conflict with this trial.
29. Evidence of active untreated systemic or serious infections (i.e., pneumonia, complicated urinary infection).
30. Body mass index (BMI) ≥40 kg/m2.

trials.title: Brain and Heart Rhythm Responses to a Breathing-Linked Sound Application (BELL-001) in Adults With Insomnia Symptoms
trials.summary: The purpose of this study was to describe how brain activity and heart rhythm respond to BELL-001, a smartphone application that plays sounds linked to the user's own breathing, compared with a sham application that looks the same but does not link its sounds to breathing. Adults with self-reported insomnia symptoms were randomly assigned to BELL-001 or to the sham application. During one laboratory visit, brain activity was recorded with electroencephalography (EEG), heart activity with electrocardiography (ECG), and breathing with a chest belt while participants rested with their eyes closed, then used the assigned application actively for 10 minutes, and then listened passively for 50 minutes. After the visit, all participants, regardless of laboratory group, used the BELL-001 application at home for 7 nights in an open-label period while wearing a smartwatch.

interventions.name: BELL-001 Digital Therapeutic
interventions.description: Smartphone-based digital therapeutic that plays sound linked to the user's breathing phase through insert earphones. In this study, the participant's own touchscreen press (inhalation) and release (exhalation) served as the breathing-phase signal during the active stage, followed by a sound sequence that slowed from the breathing rate established in the active stage. A respiration belt was used for recording only and was not an input to the application.

interventions.name: Sham Digital Therapeutic
interventions.description: Application with the same appearance and screen flow as BELL-001 that plays a single fixed pre-recorded sound not linked to breathing, with brief tones at random intervals during the active stage to match the touch task.

arms.label: BELL-001
arms.description: Participants used the BELL-001 smartphone application during one laboratory visit, with sound delivered through insert earphones. After a short practice, a brief auditory evoked potential recording and 10 minutes of eyes-closed rest, participants completed a 10-minute active stage in which they held the touchscreen pressed during each inhalation and released it during each exhalation while the application played sounds that followed this press-and-release signal, and then a 50-minute passive listening stage in which the pace of the sound slowed gradually from the breathing rate established in the active stage. Eyes remained closed throughout the recording. After the visit, participants used BELL-001 at home for 7 nights in an open-label period, as did participants in the sham group.

arms.label: Sham
arms.description: Participants used a sham application with the same appearance and screen flow during one laboratory visit, with the same practice, auditory evoked potential recording and 10 minutes of eyes-closed rest. During the 10-minute active stage, they tapped the touchscreen each time they heard a brief tone presented at random intervals of 2 to 12 seconds. During the 50-minute passive stage, a single fixed pre-recorded sound that was not linked to breathing was played. Eyes remained closed throughout the recording. After the visit, participants in this group also used the BELL-001 application (not the sham) at home for 7 nights in an open-label period while wearing a wrist-worn smartwatch.

trials.eligibility:
Inclusion Criteria:

* Age 19 to 39 years
* Self-reported insomnia symptoms with an Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) score greater than 10
* Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS) score of 15 or less
* Able to provide written informed consent

Exclusion Criteria:

* Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) score of 16 or higher, or Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7) score of 16 or higher

trials.title: Developing Virtual Reality Programs to Address Social Skills Deficits in Youth With ADHD
trials.summary: Researchers at OpenMindXR, in collaboration with Indiana University, are conducting a paid research study evaluating an innovative virtual reality (VR)-based intervention designed to support social and emotional skill development in children and adolescents with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). Children with ADHD often experience challenges in social functioning, emotional regulation, and peer relationships. While behavioral therapies and school-based interventions can be effective, access, engagement, and real-world generalization of skills remain ongoing challenges. This study aims to evaluate the usability and preliminary effectiveness of VR programs for youth with ADHD.

The Perspective Taking subscale ranges from 0 to 28. The change from baseline to Day 30 is calculated as Day 30 score - Baseline score.

Higher scores indicate more improved perspective taking after the VR intervention.

The Empathic Concern subscale ranges from 0 to 28. The change from baseline to Day 30 is calculated as Day 30 score - Baseline score. primary_outcomes.measure: Overall score from Modified System Usability Scale (SUS)

trials.title: Cognitive Effects of Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy (HBOT) After a Traumatic Brain Injury
conditions: Adults Who Sustained a Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI)
Adults Who Treated With a Course of Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy
trials.summary: This is a retrospective, single-center observational study evaluating the cognitive effects of hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) in adults who sustained a traumatic brain injury (TBI). Earlier randomized controlled work at this center demonstrated cognitive improvement after HBOT in patients with chronic deficits following mild TBI. This study evaluates a large sample size and operationalizes HBOT treatment as a continuous variable in the form of a cumulative oxygen dose, something has not been done before. Using the medical records of patients treated at the Sagol Center for Hyperbaric Medicine and Research at Shamir Medical Center between 2008 and 2026, the investigators compare computerized NeuroTrax cognitive assessments obtained before and after HBOT. The investigators quantify within-patient change across the cognitive domains and the Global Cognitive Score, and test whether the magnitude of cognitive change is associated with cumulative oxygen dose, expressed as the area under the pressure-time curve (ATA-minutes). The study includes patients across all TBI severity grades and adjusts for baseline performance, age, sex, and injury severity.

trials.title: EXercise-induced PhysioLogical Adaptations In Neurological Disorders
trials.summary:
The goal of this study is to investigate how a one-time exercise session influences different parameters of brain function in people with neurological diseases compared to healthy volunteers. The main questions the study aims to answer are:

* How do fitness level, exercise performance, and physical exhaustion differ between patients with neurological diseases and healthy participants?
* How does acute exercise affect brain function and other physiological biomarkers in participants with neurological diseases?

Participants will take part in a single, one-day study visit and will be asked to:

* Perform a standardized exercise test on a bicycle ergometer
* Undergo a brain MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) scan, a blood draw, and autonomic measurements before and after the exercise test

trials.title: Postsurgical Pain and Opioid Use in Older Adults: Effects of Mild Cognitive Impairment
trials.summary: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) affects a substantial proportion of older adults undergoing major surgery and may alter pain processing, pain experience, and opioid use after surgery. This prospective observational cohort study will compare older adults with MCI and cognitively intact older adults undergoing major orthopedic and complex spine procedures. Participants will undergo preoperative assessment of cognitive function, quantitative sensory testing, heart rate variability, clinical pain, and biomarkers associated with Alzheimer's disease risk. Postoperative pain trajectories, opioid use, pain responsiveness, and cognitive outcomes will be evaluated for six months following surgery. The study aims to determine whether MCI is associated with differences in postoperative pain and opioid use outcomes and whether APOE4 status and plasma amyloid beta 42/40 ratio contribute to observed differences.

trials.title: Prospective Longitudinal Study of Sleep, Brain Activity, and Plasma Analyses in Patients Undergoing Epilepsy Surgery
trials.summary:
The goal of this observational study is to understand how sleep and brain activity change after epilepsy surgery in adults with drug-resistant epilepsy. Drug-resistant epilepsy means that seizures continue despite treatment with appropriate medications.

The study will investigate whether changes in sleep and brain activity are related to seizure control, sleep quality, and quality of life after surgery.

The main questions it aims to answer are:

* How do sleep patterns and brain activity change after epilepsy surgery?
* How are changes in sleep and brain activity related to seizure control and quality of life?
* Do sleep patterns after surgery become more like those of healthy adults?
* How are changes in blood proteins related to sleep, brain activity, and seizure control? Researchers will follow 30 adults undergoing epilepsy surgery. Their sleep will be compared with that of 10 healthy adults of similar age and sex. Healthy participants will complete the study assessments once.

Participants undergoing epilepsy surgery will complete the assessments before surgery and approximately 2 and 6 months after surgery.

At each assessment, participants will:

* Wear a small device (actigraph) on their wrist for about 2 weeks to measure sleep and activity and keep a sleep diary.
* Spend 2 consecutive nights at a patient hotel while their sleep and brain activity are recorded using polysomnography (PSG), a test that measures sleep, breathing, and brain activity.
* Answer questionnaires about sleep quality, insomnia, mood, and quality of life.
* Provide blood samples for research. Researchers will also collect information about seizure frequency, medications, and medical history.

The sleep recordings will be used to study several aspects of sleep, including:

* Sleep architecture: how much time participants spend in different stages of sleep and how often their sleep is interrupted.
* Sleep spindles and slow oscillations: patterns of brain activity during sleep that are involved in how the brain processes and organizes information.
* Cyclic alternating pattern (CAP): a measure of brief changes in brain activity during sleep that can provide information about sleep stability.
* Epileptiform activity: abnormal electrical activity in the brain that may be associated with epilepsy and can occur during sleep.

Researchers will also analyze proteins in blood samples to explore whether biological changes are related to sleep and seizure outcomes.

Epilepsy surgery and other medical treatments will be decided by the participants' treating healthcare teams, independently of this study. The study will observe changes before and after surgery without assigning participants to a treatment.

trials.title: Sleep MAPP in the Polytrauma/TBI System of Care
trials.summary: This pilot implementation trial will evaluate the Sleep Disorder Management Assistance for Providers and Patients (Sleep MAPP) Care Pathway in one Veterans Health Administration Polytrauma/TBI System of Care clinic. The care pathway combines a provider-facing decision-support tool that supports pre-visit administration and documentation of the Insomnia Severity Index with training and implementation support for clinic providers to deliver Brief Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia. The study will assess the feasibility and acceptability of the care pathway; describe changes in guideline-concordant insomnia screening and behavioral treatment; and describe preliminary changes in insomnia symptoms, neurobehavioral symptoms, and participation in social roles among Veterans with mild traumatic brain injury who receive Brief Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia. Up to 30 clinic providers or staff and 50 Veterans will be invited to complete research surveys and interviews. Implementation and clinical outcomes will be obtained from routinely collected clinical data.

interventions.name: Sleep MAPP Care Pathway
interventions.description: The Sleep MAPP Care Pathway includes four components: (1) the Sleep MAPP clinical decision-support tool, which identifies Veterans who may benefit from insomnia screening and provides clinicians with screening results and care prompts; (2) insomnia screening using the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI); (3) training PNS rehabilitation clinicians to deliver Brief Behavioral Treatment for Insomnia (BBTI); and (4) delivery of BBTI to clinically appropriate Veterans as part of routine care. BBTI is a brief, evidence-based behavioral treatment for insomnia that includes sleep education, stimulus control, sleep restriction, and strategies to support adherence and maintenance of treatment gains.

arms.label: Sleep MAPP Care Pathway
arms.description: The participating Polytrauma/TBI System of Care clinic will implement the Sleep MAPP Care Pathway, which is designed to increase delivery of two guideline-recommended clinical practices: insomnia screening with the Insomnia Severity Index and Brief Behavioral Treatment for Insomnia (BBTI). Implementation will be supported by a multicomponent strategy bundle that includes deployment of the Sleep MAPP clinical decision support tool, training providers to deliver BBTI, and complementary implementation supports.

trials.title: Parkinson's Disease in Type 1 Gaucher Disease
trials.summary: Parkinson's disease (PD) is an age-related movement disorder with a complex pathophysiology. Among the risk factors for PD, variants in beta-glucocerebrosidase (encoded by the gene GBA1) represent one of the most significant heritable risk factors for lifetime PD risk. Biallelic variants in GBA1 cause Gaucher disease (GD), a multisystem disorder, and individuals with late/adult-onset GD1 have a \~1-in-9 lifetime risk for PD. This study aims to develop a cross-sectional cohort of clinical and laboratory phenotyped adult GD1 patients and controls for investigation of clinical/laboratory risk factors for current and future Parkinson risk. Neurological evaluations will be video and audio recorded to allow the investigators to quantify neurological function using automated tools. Data and specimens generated in this study will be incorporated into a de-identified biobank that will be used for further research into GD and PD.

arms.label: GD1 Patients
arms.description: 80 GD1 patients (with or without PD) from Mount Sinai health system and partnering Gaucher Disease treatment programs.

arms.label: GBA1 Heterozygotes
arms.description: 10 GBA1 heterozygote individuals, preferably relatives of GD1 patients.

arms.label: Neurologically Healthy Non-GBA1-Carriers
arms.description: 10 non-carriers for GBA1 without neurological disorder and no first degree family relative with PD.

primary_outcomes.measure: Movement Disorder Society Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS): Parts I, II, and IV
primary_outcomes.description: The MDS-UPDRS is a standardized clinical assessment used by neurologists to study PD. Three parts (I/II/IV) are used to evaluate individuals' symptoms of Parkinson's Disease, including non-motor and motor experiences of daily living and common PD comorbidities. Each part contains several items (each rated by severity on a 0 to 4 scale) Part I (subscale from 0-52), Part II (subscale from 0-52), and Part IV (subscale from 0-24) are summed for a total score from 0-128. A higher score indicates higher severity of PD-related symptoms.

primary_outcomes.measure: REM Behavioral Disorder Screening Questionnaire (RBDSQ)
primary_outcomes.description: RBDSQ is a simple 10-item yes/no response screening questionnaire to screen for REM sleep behavior disorders, a known risk factor for PD. The range for this scale is 0 to 13 points. Each item contributes 1 point except a single item that contributes 4 points for up to four specific manifestations of REM Behavior Disorders. A score of 5 or higher indicates a positive screening threshold for REM Behavioral Disorder (RBD).

primary_outcomes.measure: Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA)
primary_outcomes.description: MoCA is a 10-minute cognitive screening tool used to detect mild-cognitive impairment (MCI) by assessing short-term memory, visuospatial abilities, executive functions, attention and concentration, working memory, language, and orientation to time and place. The scale ranges from 0 to 30 points. Severe impairment scores between 0-9 and normal cognitive performance scored at 26 and above. The higher the score, the less cognitive impairment.

primary_outcomes.measure: Scales for Outcomes in Parkinson's Disease - Autonomic Dysfunction (SCOPA-AUT)
primary_outcomes.description: SCOPA-AUT is a 25-item questionnaire used to assess autonomic symptoms (gastrointestinal, urinary, cardiovascular, thermoregulatory, pupillomotor, sexual) in patients with Parkinson's disease. This scale includes subscales for gastrointestinal (0-7), urinary (0-6), cardiovascular (0-3), thermoregulatory (0-4), pupillomotor (0-1), and sexual (2 items for men and 2 items for women) symptoms. Total scale ranges from 0-23 where a higher score in any or total symptoms indicates higher severity.

primary_outcomes.measure: University of Pennsylvania Smell Identification Test (UPSIT)
primary_outcomes.description: UPSIT is a reliable 40-item test of olfactory function using microencapsulated odorants which are released by scratching scent strips across four small booklets. The individual then picks the answer from a list of four multiple-choice options. The final score is the number of correct answers between 0 and 40. A lower score indicates olfactory dysfunction, and a higher score indicates a more normal sense of smell.

primary_outcomes.measure: Movement Disorder Society-Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS) Part III
primary_outcomes.description: This section includes 18 items assessing tone, tremor, gait, movement, and posture at various sites of the body which are all rated on a scale of 0 to 4, with 4 indicating more severe symptoms. It also includes four yes/no questions regarding current medication / treatment for ongoing dyskinesia during the examination as well as a single 0 to 5 rating on overall functional status, with higher ratings reflecting greater functional impairment. The score ranges from 0-133 with higher score indicating more severe impairment.

trials.title: Adapting the Sensory Environment to Reduce Stress in Children With Autism During Dental Visits
trials.summary:
This study aims to evaluate the impact of a sensory-adapted dental environment (SADE) on the stress levels and behavioral responses of children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) during dental visits.

Children with ASD often experience sensory sensitivities, making traditional dental care challenging and stressful. In this study, 40 children aged 8 to 12 diagnosed with ASD, along with their parents or legal guardians, will participate in two standard dental visits spaced 30 days apart. The first visit will take place under standard clinical conditions, while the second visit will utilize a sensory-adapted dental environment featuring modified visual elements (such as dark protective glasses), auditory (noise-canceling headphones or relaxing music), taste (unflavored toothpaste), smell (sweet orange essential oil) and tactile adjustments (a weighted blanket).

The study will measure stress using objective tools, including continuous digital biomarkers of stress recorded via wristbands (such as heart rate, electrodermal activity, accelerometer data, actigraphy, movement intensity, step count, metabolic equivalent of task, skin temperature, and peripheral body orientation) and the analysis of salivary lysozyme and cortisol levels in both children and parents. Additionally, standardized psychological questionnaires will be used to assess the child's sensory profile, as well as parental stress and coping strategies. The findings will help determine whether modifying the sensory environment can effectively reduce anxiety and improve the dental care experience for children with autism.

interventions.name: Sensory-Adapted Dental Environment
interventions.description: A multi-sensory adaptation of the dental operatory applied during the second study visit (Visit 2). The modification includes five components: visual (yellow-filtered operating lamp and dark protective glasses), auditory (noise-canceling headphones or relaxing music), tactile (a weighted blanket), olfactory (sweet orange essential oil diffusion), and gustatory (unflavored prophylaxis toothpaste). The first visit serves as the control condition using a Regular Dental Environment (RDE) without these modifications.

arms.label: SADE Intervention Group
arms.description: A prospective, single-arm, non-randomized interventional study where all participating complete two sequential, standardized afternoon dental visits spaced 30 days apart. Visit 1 is conducted under standard clinical conditions (Regular Dental Environment - RDE) on a clinical chair without modifications, serving as the baseline reference. Visit 2 is conducted in a single-chair operatory utilizing a Sensory-Adapted Dental Environment (SADE) featuring multi-sensory adjustments. Both visits involve dental procedures performed by the same pediatric dentist, alongside real-time physiologic stress monitoring (via Empatica EmbracePlus wristbands), salivary sample collection (lysozyme and cortisol assays), pictorial self-report mood assessments, and psychological questionnaires (custom SMILED Scale, SSP-2, PSI-IV, CISS, STAI).

primary_outcomes.description: Continuous recording of skin conductance (in microSiemens, μS) via Empatica EmbracePlus to to measure child physiological stress during dental visits in RDE versus SADE conditions.
primary_outcomes.timeFrame: Measured continuously in real-time during both dental visits (Visit 1 and Visit 2), approx. 30-90 minutes per visit.

primary_outcomes.description: Continuous recording of actigraphy data derived from the tri-axial accelerometer (in gravitational force units, g) to assess child physical restlessness during dental visits in RDE versus SADE conditions.

trials.eligibility:
Inclusion Criteria:

1. Child Inclusion Criteria

   * Age: 8-12 years.
   * Diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD): Official ASD diagnosis according to ICD-10, ICD-11, or DSM-5 criteria, confirmed by medical documentation from a psychiatrist/pediatric psychiatrist, a psychologist's opinion, or a diagnostic team.
   * No Prior Contact: No prior contact with the proposed intervention (e.g., the specific calming techniques used in the study).
   * Absence of Profound Cognitive Deficits: Required level of intellectual functioning: IQ \> 70.

2. Parent/Legal Guardian Inclusion Criteria

   * Role and Age: Parent or legal guardian of the minor participant diagnosed with ASD, aged over 18 years.
   * Consent to Participate: Written informed consent obtained from the parent/legal guardian as a study participant.
   * Health Status: Stable mental and somatic health status over the last 30 days.

Exclusion Criteria:

1. Child Exclusion Criteria

   * Current Anxiety Treatment: Child undergoing psychological or pharmacological therapy directly aimed at treating anxiety (e.g., CBT, anti-anxiety medications).
   * Changes in Psychotropic Medication: Initiation of a new psychotropic drug or dosage change within the 4 weeks prior to the study.
   * Diagnosis of Other Mental Disorders: Schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorders, or bipolar affective disorders that could interfere with the study.
   * Clinically Significant Suicidal Ideation: Present currently or in the recent history.
   * Persistent Aggression or Self-Aggression: Behaviors that may prevent the safe execution of the dental procedure.
   * Somatic Comorbidities Co-occurring with ASD: Conditions that may increase stress-related risks, such as pharmacologically uncontrolled epilepsy, heart failure, unstable type 1 diabetes, or central nervous system disorders.
   * Significant Family Life Instability: Within the last 4 weeks (e.g., relocation, divorce, crisis interventions).
   * Oral Pain or Salivary Disorders: Dental pain originating from the oral cavity or salivary gland secretion disorders in the child.
   * Lack of Consent: Absence of written consent from the parent/legal guardian or lack of the child's assent to participate.
   * Upper Respiratory Tract Infection: Occurring within the last 7 days.
2. Parent/Legal Guardian Exclusion Criteria

   * Lack of Consent: Absence of written consent from the parent/legal guardian to participate as a study subject.
   * Oral Pain or Salivary Disorders: Dental pain originating from the oral cavity or salivary gland secretion disorders in the parent/legal guardian.
   * Severe Mental Function Disorders: Diagnosed severe mental impairment requiring therapy with high doses of neurotropic drugs.
   * Significant Family Life Instability: Within the last 4 weeks (e.g., relocation, divorce, crisis interventions).
   * Upper Respiratory Tract Infection: Occurring within the last 7 days. Because the study is conducted in parent-child dyads, the refusal or withdrawal of consent by one participant automatically excludes the other from the study.

trials.title: Deep Brain Stimulation Guided by Brain Mapping to Treat Cognitive Impairment
conditions: Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) Due to Alzheimer's Disease
trials.summary:
This trial is a 12-month safety and feasibility study, enrolling up to six participants. These participants will serve as their own controls, structured in multiple parts that follow an initial short-term stereo electroencephalography (SEEG) mapping period.

During this trial we aim to demonstrate the safety of acute and chronic network-guided stimulation in Mild Cognitive Impairment by evaluating adverse effects, tolerability, and feasibility during both the short- term SEEG mapping phase and subsequent permanent DBS therapy.

In addition to safety measures, therapeutic results as follows are to be tested for: (1) Develop patient-specific stimulation parameters for the treatment of MCI, as well as develop and test memory state classifiers by enrolling six individuals to undergo intracranial mapping (SEEG). We will use targeted memory tasks to generate neural data needed for state distinctions, and conduct a systematic parameter search to identify and develop optimal settings for each patient. (2) Assess efficacy of open loop stimulation by delivering a fixed open loop protocol based on the parameters discovered earlier, while SEEG electrodes remain in place, and testing the efficacy of the trained classifier to detect favorable brain states. (3) Evaluate chronic DBS therapy by implanting a permanent system in participants who show an acute beneficial response to assess long term outcomes. (4) Assess therapeutic outcomes and refine protocols by measuring reductions in memory-related impairment.

The above findings will guide further refinement of the device and protocol.

primary_outcomes.measure: Demonstrate device safety
primary_outcomes.description: Description: The primary objective is to demonstrate safety of acute and chronic network guided stimulation for Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI). This is determined if participants with the Deep Brain Stimulation Device demonstrate no significant device related serious adverse events (SAE). Device safety will be measured by number of reported SAE's in years 2 through 4.

trials.eligibility:
Inclusion Criteria:

1. Men and women (non-pregnant) between ages 60 and 85.
2. Meets NIA-AA core clinical criteria for MCI due to Alzheimer's Disease.
3. Determination by the investigator, based on clinical judgment and review of medical history, neurological examination, cognitive profile, and available clinical data, that Alzheimer's Disease is the primary suspected etiology.
4. Absence of other psychiatric or physical conditions that could interfere with the study.
5. Stable medication regimen for 4 weeks preceding surgery; participants currently receiving anti-amyloid therapies may enroll if they are able and willing to pause infusions for at least 12 weeks prior to study initiation and for the duration of the study.
6. Other medical conditions must be stable for at least 6 months prior to SEEG Implantation.
7. Able and willing to give informed consent or have a Legally Authorized Representative who is able to sign the informed consent form.
8. Able to have a study partner(s) or close relative(s) present for discussions about the study

Exclusion Criteria:

1. Active alcohol or substance use disorder within 6 months of entering the Screening Phase, excluding nicotine. Urine drug test positive for illicit drugs.
2. Neurological/Medical condition that makes the participant, in the opinion of the surgeon, a poor surgical candidate (e.g., progressive neurodegenerative disorder, significant cardiopulmonary disorder, need for chronic anticoagulation).
3. Any history of seizure disorder, hemorrhagic stroke, or has high risk of seizure (history of congenital brain malformation, neuro-developmental disorder , or other factors that predispose seizures such as an active eating disorder).
4. Cognitive symptoms that are not be better explained by delirium, unstable psychiatric illness, active substance use disorder, major untreated sleep disorder, acute neurologic illness, or other medical condition that, in the investigator's judgment, is the primary cause of the impairment.
5. Brain structural MRI abnormalities outside of expected pathology associated with Mild Cognitive Impairment.
6. Any medical contraindication to surgery such as infection.
7. Coagulopathy: Bleeding propensity and/or one of the following: INR \> 1.5; prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) ≥ 45 sec; platelet count \< 100×103 /uL
8. Uncontrolled hypertension (systolic \> 145mmHg and/or diastolic \> 90 mmHg), demonstrated on each of three repeated measurements taken within one hour regardless of whether or not the participant is taking antihypertensive medications.
9. Participation in another drug, device, or biological study within 90 days.
10. Current implanted neural stimulation devices including spinal cord stimulators and deep brain stimulators.
11. Need for Diathermy.
12. Chronic use of anticoagulant or anti-platelet agents that cannot be safely stopped for a sufficient duration (minimum 2.5 weeks) in the peri-operative period.
13. Any Psychiatric/Neurological/Medical condition that makes the participant, in the opinion of the Investigator, a poor candidate. These may be but are not limited to a DSM-5 diagnosis of schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder.
14. Moderate to severe depressive symptoms, defined as a GDS-15 score ≥11 at screening, or investigator judgment that depressive symptoms are unstable, severe, or likely to interfere with study participation or interpretation of cognitive outcomes.
15. High risk of suicide, defined as any of the following on the Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS) short form at screening: active suicidal ideation with intent to act, active suicidal ideation with a specific plan and intent, suicidal behavior within the past 3 months or investigator judgment that the participant is at imminent or clinically significant risk for self-harm.
16. A separate cardiac condition that, in the opinion of a study physician, would present an unacceptable risk of undergoing general anesthesia.
17. Any clinical impression reflective of disease pathologies indicated by the list below is exclusionary

    1. Frontotemporal degeneration spectrum disorders (e.g., behavioral-variant FTD, primary progressive aphasia)
    2. Dementia with Lewy bodies / Parkinson disease dementia
    3. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (moderate to severe)

Eligibility Note:

Participants will be excluded if the investigator determines that cognitive impairment is primarily attributable to vascular cognitive impairment, Lewy body disease, frontotemporal degeneration, Parkinson's disease, traumatic brain injury, delirium, unstable psychiatric illness, medication effects, substance use, or another non-AD neurologic or systemic condition.

A prior or concurrent diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease is permitted only if the participant is clinically at the MCI / mild neurocognitive disorder stage, rather than dementia stage. In other words, participants with "MCI due to Alzheimer's disease," "prodromal Alzheimer's disease," or "early Alzheimer's disease" may be included if functional independence is preserved.

trials.title: Multimodal Rehabilitation and Balance Assessment in Parkinson's Disease
trials.summary:
This study aimed to investigate the relationship between instrumented balance measurements and clinical balance assessments in individuals with Parkinson's disease and to evaluate changes in balance and functional mobility following a 12-week multimodal rehabilitation program.

Eighteen individuals with Parkinson's disease participated in this prospective, single-group study. All participants received a rehabilitation program that included balance exercises, aerobic exercise, and balance training using the Korebalance system. The program was conducted twice weekly for 12 weeks.

Balance was assessed using the Korebalance system and the Berg Balance Scale (BBS). Functional mobility was evaluated using the Timed Up and Go (TUG) test. Assessments were performed before and after the rehabilitation program.

The study examined whether instrumented balance measurements were associated with clinical balance performance and whether balance and functional mobility changed following rehabilitation.

interventions.name: Multimodal Rehabilitation Program
interventions.description: Participants received a supervised multimodal rehabilitation program twice weekly for 12 weeks (24 sessions). The program included approximately 10 minutes of warm-up exercises, 20 minutes of progressive balance training, and 20 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise using a treadmill or stationary bicycle. Balance exercises included static and dynamic balance tasks, multidirectional stepping, functional mobility activities, turning, and dual-task training. Additional balance training was performed using the Korebalance Premiere-19 system. Exercise intensity was generally maintained at a Borg Rating of Perceived Exertion of 11-14. Exercises were individually progressed according to participant ability and safety.

arms.label: Multimodal Rehabilitation Group
arms.description: Participants with Parkinson's disease received a 12-week supervised multimodal rehabilitation program, conducted twice weekly. The intervention included progressive balance exercises, functional mobility training, dual-task activities, moderate-intensity aerobic exercise, and Korebalance-assisted balance training. All participants received the same intervention, with no control group.

primary_outcomes.measure: Change in Static Korebalance Score
primary_outcomes.description: Static balance was assessed using the Korebalance Premiere-19 system. Measurements were obtained at baseline and after the 12-week multimodal rehabilitation program. Lower scores indicate better balance performance. Change was calculated as the post-intervention score minus the baseline score.

primary_outcomes.measure: Change in Dynamic Korebalance Score
primary_outcomes.description: Dynamic balance was assessed using the Korebalance Premiere-19 system. Measurements were obtained at baseline and after the 12-week multimodal rehabilitation program. Lower scores indicate better balance performance. Change was calculated as the post-intervention score minus the baseline score.

Exclusion Criteria:

* Significant cognitive impairment that could interfere with participation or assessment.
* Other neurological disorders affecting balance or mobility.
* History of surgery within the preceding six months.

trials.title: Study of the Link Between Structural Alterations in the Hypothalamus and Cardiac Dysautonomia in Drug-resistant Epilepsy
trials.summary: Patients with drug-resistant epilepsy may have cardiac dysautonomia, with reduced heart rate variability and increased sympathetic tone. This condition is part of the concept of "epileptic heart" and could be a risk factor for sudden death, one of the main causes of excess mortality in patients with severe epilepsy in adulthood. The mechanism of this cardiac impairment is poorly understood. The hypothalamus, due to its role as the subcortical conductor of the autonomic nervous system and its known links with the limbic system, particularly the amygdala and hippocampus, is a candidate for a key intermediary role in the impact of seizures on cardiorespiratory function. The investigators wish to investigate the hypothesis that cardiac dysautonomia in patients with drug-resistant epilepsy is correlated with structural changes in the hypothalamus. The investigators wish to study in 7Tesla MRI the volume of the different hypothalamic nuclei, the amygdalo- hypothalamic and hypothalamo-bulbar connectivity, as well as the metabolic content in spectroscopy in patients with drug-resistant epilepsy, and correlate these data with the sympathetic and parasympathetic tones of these patients.

interventions.name: MRI scan
interventions.description:
Patients will be recruited and included by the epileptologist in the clinical neurophysiology department, after verification of the inclusion criteria. The patient will then undergo an MRI scan on the 7T machine at Lille University Hospital during the Amiens shifts.

The anonymized images will be transmitted to Amiens-Picardie University Hospital via an existing secure system. The images will be processed in Amiens under the supervision of Prof.

Constans.

interventions.name: electrocardiogram
interventions.description: Heart rate variability parameters will be calculated from the patients' electrocardiograms, performed as part of their care under the supervision of Prof. Szurhaj.

primary_outcomes.measure: Correlation coefficient between the volume of the posterior hypothalamic nucleus with the degree of cardiac autonomic function impairment
primary_outcomes.description: Correlation coefficient between the volume of the posterior hypothalamic nucleus with the degree of cardiac autonomic function impairment across the entire cohort of patients with epilepsy

trials.title: Physical Activity, Sleep Quality, and Respiratory Function in Obstructive Sleep Apnea
trials.summary: Although exercise and physical activity have shown beneficial effects in individuals with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), evidence regarding the effects of daily physical activity habits on sleep quality and respiratory parameters remains limited. This study aims to investigate these associations in individuals with OSA.

interventions.name: Physical Activity Education
interventions.description: Participants will receive physical activity education supported by illustrated materials and brochures. Recommendations will include: (1) aerobic exercise, with at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity weekly (e.g., walking or cycling) over at least 3 days; (2) muscle-strengthening exercises targeting major muscle groups 2-3 days per week, with 3 sets of 8-15 repetitions; (3) balance and flexibility exercises 3 days per week; and (4) diaphragmatic breathing exercises for 15-30 minutes per session, 3 days per week. Exercise sessions will include 5-10 minutes of warm-up and cool-down. Periodic follow-up contacts will encourage adherence throughout the 24-week intervention. All participants will continue prescribed CPAP therapy.

arms.label: Control Group (CG)
arms.description: Participants will continue using physician-prescribed continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy and will be instructed to use CPAP every night for 24 weeks. No additional physical activity education will be provided as part of the study intervention.

arms.label: Physical Activity Education Group (PAEG)
arms.description: Participants will receive physical activity education at baseline, supported by visual materials and brochures. The education will include moderate-intensity aerobic and muscle-strengthening activities in accordance with established physical activity guidelines. Participants will be contacted periodically to assess adherence to physical activity recommendations. Participants will continue their prescribed CPAP therapy throughout the 24-week study period.

primary_outcomes.measure: Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI)
primary_outcomes.description: A 19-item self-report questionnaire assessing sleep quality and disturbances over the previous month, including sleep duration, latency, efficiency, and daytime dysfunction. Total scores range from 0 to 21, with higher scores indicating poorer sleep quality. Scores above 5 indicate poor sleep quality.

primary_outcomes.measure: CPAP Adherence Data
primary_outcomes.description: CPAP device data will be downloaded to assess average nightly usage, mask leak, and treatment pressure. Good adherence will be defined as CPAP use for at least 4 hours per night on at least 5 nights per week.

primary_outcomes.measure: MIP-MEP measurement
primary_outcomes.description: In centimeters of water (cmH2O), it will be obtained using a Respiratory Muscle Strength Measurement Device-MIP-MEP (MD Diagnostics Ltd., RP Check, United Kingdom) in accordance with the recommendations of the American Thoracic Society.

primary_outcomes.measure: Forced Vital Capacity (FVC) measurement
primary_outcomes.description:
It is the amount of air expelled after maximum inspiration following a normal breath, expressed in liters. While healthy individuals can forcefully exhale air for 2-3 seconds, this time can be as short as 10-15 seconds for individuals with airway problems. At the end of the test, the expected reference value should be between 80-120%.

This will be performed using a spirometer (Cosmed, Pony FX, Italy). The best forced vital capacity (FVC) maneuver from at least 3 attempts will be selected according to the criteria of the American Thoracic Society. To perform the spirometric maneuvers, participants will sit upright with their feet on the floor and the nose clip correctly positioned.

primary_outcomes.measure: FEV₁ (Forced Expiratory Volume in 1 Second)
primary_outcomes.description:
It is the volume of air exhaled in the first second after forced expiration. Although measured in liters, it actually indicates the airflow rate. In healthy individuals, at least 72% of the air should be exhaled, reflecting the function of the large airways.

This will be performed using a spirometer (Cosmed, Pony FX, Italy). To perform the spirometric maneuvers, participants will sit upright with their feet on the floor and the nose clip correctly positioned.

primary_outcomes.measure: FEV1/FVC ratio
primary_outcomes.description:
This ratio is obtained by dividing FEV1 by FVC and evaluates airway patency and lung function. In a normal individual, this ratio is around 70-80%.

This will be performed using a spirometer (Cosmed, Pony FX, Italy). To perform the spirometric maneuvers, participants will sit upright with their feet on the floor and the nose clip correctly positioned.

primary_outcomes.measure: FEF 25%-75% (Maximal Mid-Expiratory Flow Rate
primary_outcomes.description:
It refers to the average airflow rate during forced expiration, when 25% to 75% of the volume is expelled. It is measured in liters per second. It reflects the function of the medium and small airways. A value above 80% of the reference value is normal.

This will be performed using a spirometer (Cosmed, Pony FX, Italy). To perform the spirometric maneuvers, participants will sit upright with their feet on the floor and the nose clip correctly positioned.

primary_outcomes.measure: Baecke Habitual Physical Activity Questionnaire (BHPAQ)
primary_outcomes.description: 16-item self-report questionnaire assessing habitual physical activity over the previous year across three domains: occupational activity (8 items), sports activity (4 items), and leisure-time activity (4 items). The total score is calculated by summing the three domain scores.

trials.eligibility:
Inclusion Criteria:

* Individuals diagnosed with mild to severe obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) based on laboratory polysomnography (AHI: 5-30 events/hour).
* Individuals diagnosed by a pulmonologist within the past year who initiated CPAP therapy no more than 12 months ago and demonstrate regular use.
* Individuals with habitual snoring.
* Individuals who have not participated in OSA-focused physiotherapy interventions within the past 3 months.

Exclusion Criteria:

* Body mass index (BMI) \>40 kg/m².
* Severe substance or alcohol dependence.
* Regular use of sedatives, muscle relaxants, or opioids that may affect sleep patterns.
* Pregnancy or postpartum period (\<6 months).
* Medical contraindications to physical activity according to American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM) guidelines, such as unstable coronary artery disease or decompensated heart failure.
* History of stroke or significant respiratory, neuromuscular, inflammatory, or other disorders causing hypercapnia.
* Craniofacial abnormalities, severe upper airway obstruction, or secondary respiratory diseases such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

trials.title: Hand Grip Strength Correlates Strongly With Weekly Working Hours - the Importance of Upper Limb Function in Multiple Sclerosis
trials.summary:
Multiple sclerosis (MS) as leading cause of non-traumatic neurological disability in young adults has additionally to the individual's burden of disease a significant influence on their ability to work.

Objective of this study is to test parameters for their correlation with weekly working hours.

We will retrospectively analyse data of people with MS (pwMS) and correlate weekly working hours with demographics, Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS), Nine Hole Peg Test (9HPT), walking speed measured by Timed 25-Foot Walk test (T25FW), Symbol Digit Modalities Test (SDMT) and Hand Grip Strength (HGS).

interventions.name: hand grip strength
interventions.description: The HGS test is a measure of upper extremity muscle strength and muscle function (17). The test was performed in seated position with lower extremities on the ground and with the elbow angle of 90 degrees. Saehan dynamometer with string mechanism and scale displaying the measured value in kilograms (kg) was used. Participants were asked to press the dynamometer as strong as possible, three times with each hand, and the highest result in each hand was recorded and subsequently the average of both hands was calculated.

primary_outcomes.measure: Correlation of routine parameters with weekly working hours
primary_outcomes.description: Correlation of Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS), Nine Hole Peg Test (9HPT), walking speed measured by Timed 25-Foot Walk test (T25FW), Symbol Digit Modalities Test (SDMT) and Hand Grip Strength (HGS) with weekly working hours

trials.eligibility:

Measurements included the 9HPT, T25FW, HGS and SDMT at least once during the study period as part of their routine examinations

trials.title: Doppler Ultrasonography Parameters and Mortality in Traumatic Brain Injury
trials.summary: The purpose of this study is to find out whether blood flow measurements of the brain and neck arteries, obtained with bedside Doppler ultrasonography are associated with neurological outcome and survival in adult patients with traumatic brain injury treated in the intensive care unit. Transcranial and carotid Doppler examinations are performed at three time points during the intensive care stay. Regional cerebral oxygen saturation is also monitored with near-infrared spectroscopy when the device is available. The study does not change patient treatment; all measurements are non-invasive and are performed alongside routine care.

interventions.name: Transcranial and Carotid Doppler Ultrasonography
interventions.description: Non-invasive bedside Doppler measurement of peak systolic velocity, end-diastolic velocity, time-averaged mean velocity, pulsatility index, and resistive index in the common carotid, internal carotid, external carotid, and middle cerebral arteries.

arms.label: Patients With Traumatic Brain Injury
arms.description: Adult patients with traumatic brain injury admitted to the intensive care unit who undergo serial transcranial and carotid Doppler ultrasonography within the first 24 hours after admission, at 72 hours, and on day 7 when clinically feasible.
interventionNames: Diagnostic Test: Transcranial and Carotid Doppler Ultrasonography

primary_outcomes.description: Middle cerebral artery pulsatility index measured by transcranial Doppler within the first 24 hours after ICU admission, at 72 hours, and on day 7 when clinically feasible will be analyzed for its association with neurological outcome assessed by the Glasgow Outcome Scale / Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended (GOS/GOSE).

trials.title: Rehabilitation Through Virtual Immersion & Integrated Exposure for Mild Traumatic Brain Injury (ReVIVE for mTBI)
conditions: Traumatic Brain Injury and Co-occurring Disorders
trials.summary: The primary goal of this study is to evaluate the effectiveness of an integrated therapeutic model - combining VR and standard psychotherapy in improving executive function and hyperarousal adults impacted with mTBI. Specifically, the study will: Evaluate PTSD Symptom Reduction - PTSD symptoms, specifically hyperarousal and hypervigilance will be assessed using the Davidson Trauma Scale, which will provide insight into improvements PTSD symptom reduction.

interventions.name: Virtual Reality
interventions.description: ReVIVE is a virtual reality (VR)-based rehabilitation intervention delivered over six weekly sessions as an adjunct to standard care for individuals with PTSD following mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI). Using an Oculus Quest VR headset, participants complete approximately 10 minutes of acclimation followed by 30 minutes of immersive activities. The intervention incorporates mindfulness, breathing and grounding exercises, emotional regulation, and cognitive and functional activities within simulated everyday environments. Scenarios are designed to support engagement with progressively more complex environments and tasks. Intervention tolerability is monitored using the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire before and after VR sessions. Standard care, including routine psychotherapy and medication management, continues throughout the study.

interventions.name: Standard Psychotherapy
interventions.description: Standard psychotherapy consists of ongoing therapy received by participants before enrollment and continued throughout the study as part of the participants usual care. Sessions focus on identifying emotions, recognizing cognitive shifts and difficulties, supporting real-time emotional and cognitive regulation, and facilitating interpersonal processing and emotional labeling. Psychotherapy frequency and treatment decisions remain at the discretion of participants' treating clinicians and are not standardized or altered by the study. Participants assigned to the control arm continue standard psychotherapy and medication management without receiving the study's virtual reality intervention.

arms.label: ReVIVE Virtual Reality + Standard Care
arms.description: Participants randomized to this arm will receive six weekly sessions of virtual reality (VR)-based rehabilitation in addition to standard care, including routine psychotherapy and medication management. Each session includes approximately 10 minutes of VR acclimation followed by 30 minutes of immersive VR activities designed to support emotional regulation, cognitive functioning, and functional rehabilitation. Activities incorporate mindfulness, breathing and grounding techniques, and everyday environments and tasks, with scenarios progressing in complexity. Intervention tolerability will be monitored using the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire administered before and after VR sessions.

arms.label: Standard Care Only
arms.description: Participants randomized to this arm will continue receiving standard care, including routine psychotherapy and medication management, without the addition of virtual reality (VR)-based rehabilitation. Participants will still complete study assessments at the scheduled time points to evaluate changes PTSD-related symptoms over the study period.

primary_outcomes.measure: Change in PTSD Symptom Severity Measured by the Davidson Trauma Scale (DTS)
primary_outcomes.description: PTSD-related symptom severity will be assessed using the 17-item Davidson Trauma Scale (DTS), a self-report measure evaluating the frequency and severity of trauma-related symptoms, including intrusion, avoidance, and hyperarousal. Changes in DTS scores will be evaluated over the study period. The DTS yields a frequency score (ranging from 0 to 68), severity score (ranging from 0 to 68), and total score (ranging from 0 to 136). Higher score worse severity/frequency.
primary_outcomes.timeFrame: Baseline, midpoint assessment at approximately 3 weeks, final post-intervention assessment approximately 1 week post completion of the six-week intervention.

trials.eligibility:
Inclusion criteria:

* History of one or more concussions.
* Presence of mild-to-moderate PTSD symptoms, defined as a score between 20 and 44 on the Davidson Trauma Scale (DTS), indicating clinically relevant but not severe symptomatology (Davidson et al., 1997).
* Prior or ongoing therapy, defined as current or recent (within the last 3 months) engagement in standard care treatments such as psychiatric medication management, and evidence-based psychotherapy targeting mTBI or PTSD symptoms.
* Prior U.S military service (any duration and any branch) is required for eligibility.

Exclusion criteria:

* Age over 55 to reduce confounding effects of age-related neurodegeneration and cognitive decline.
* Diagnosis of severe psychiatric disorders (e.g., schizophrenia, bipolar disorder).
* Active substance abuse.
* Presence of unrelated neurological conditions such as epilepsy, stroke, seizure disorders, or neurodegenerative diseases (e.g., Alzheimer's, Parkinson's).
* Significant cognitive impairment, assessed by standardized cognitive screening, which would interfere with the ability to participate fully in VR and therapy sessions.
* Physical impairments that would prevent safe engagement in VR and therapy.

trials.title: Danang Cerebral Venous Thrombosis Registry
trials.summary:
Cerebral venous thrombosis (CVT) is an uncommon but potentially life-threatening type of stroke, predominantly affecting young adults and women. Although prompt diagnosis and anticoagulant therapy can lead to favorable outcomes, data regarding the clinical spectrum, neuroimaging patterns, risk factors, and long-term functional recovery of CVT patients in central Vietnam remain limited.

This prospective observational study aims to establish a hospital-based registry to investigate the clinical characteristics, neuroimaging features, etiology, and treatment outcomes of patients diagnosed with cerebral venous thrombosis at Danang Hospital.

All consecutive patients with confirmed CVT admitted to Danang Hospital are enrolled and managed according to standard clinical protocols. Participants are monitored throughout their hospital stay to assess acute manifestations, imaging abnormalities (on CT/CTV or MRI/MRV), and inpatient complications. Functional outcomes and recovery are evaluated at hospital discharge and during follow-up using the modified Rankin Scale (mRS).

interventions.name: Standard Anticoagulant Therapy
interventions.description: Patients receive therapeutic anticoagulation according to standard clinical guidelines (low-molecular-weight heparin or unfractionated heparin in the acute phase, followed by oral anticoagulants including vitamin K antagonists or direct oral anticoagulants), along with supportive medical care and endovascular treatment when indicated.

arms.label: CVT cohort
arms.description: All consecutive adult patients diagnosed with cerebral venous thrombosis (confirmed by CTV or MRV) admitted to Danang Hospital and followed up for clinical characteristics, neuroimaging features, and functional outcomes.

primary_outcomes.measure: Favorable Functional Outcome Assessed by the Modified Rankin Scale (mRS)
primary_outcomes.description: Functional status is evaluated using the modified Rankin Scale (mRS), a standardized clinical tool measuring the degree of disability or dependence in daily activities. The scale ranges from 0 (no symptoms) to 6 (death). A favorable functional outcome is defined as an mRS score of 0 to 1 (complete recovery or no significant disability despite symptoms)

trials.eligibility:
Inclusion Criteria:

1. Age 18 years or older.
2. Definite diagnosis of cerebral venous thrombosis confirmed by neuroimaging, including computed tomography venography (CTV), magnetic resonance venography (MRV), or digital subtraction angiography (DSA).
3. Admitted to Danang Hospital for acute or subacute management.
4. Patient or legally authorized representative provides written informed consent to participate in the registry.

Exclusion Criteria:

1. Non-thrombotic occlusion of cerebral veins or sinuses (e.g., direct tumor invasion, vascular malformation, or extrinsic mechanical compression without thrombosis).
2. Pre-existing advanced terminal illness or severe co-morbid condition with a life expectancy of less than 6 months prior to CVT presentation (e.g., end-stage malignancy, advanced organ failure).
3. pre-mRS ≥ 2
4. Inability or refusal of the patient or their legal representative to complete the 6-month follow-up assessment.
5. Refusal to provide informed consent.

Title: Brain Imaging of Childhood Onset Psychiatric Disorders, Endocrine Disorders and Healthy Volunteers
Conditions: Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, Schizophrenia, Attention Deficit Disorder With Hyperactivity
Brief summary: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) unlike X-rays and CT-scans does not use radiation to create a picture. MRI use as the name implies, magnetism to create pictures with excellent anatomical resolution. Functional MRIs are diagnostic tests that allow doctors to not only view anatomy, but physiology and function. It is for these reasons that MRIs are excellent methods for studying the brain.

In this study, researchers will use MRI to assess brain anatomy and function in X and Y chromosome variation, healthy volunteers, and patients with a variety of childhood onset psychiatric disorders. The disorders include attention deficit disorder, autism, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, childhood-onset schizophrenia, dyslexia, obsessive compulsive disorder, Sydenham's chorea, and Tourette's syndrome.

Results of the MRIs showing the anatomy of the brain and brain function will be compared across age, sex (gender), and diagnostic groups. Correlations between brain

chunks.text:
Title: Aging Stereotypes and Prodromal Alzheimer's Disease
Conditions: Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI)
Brief summary: Because of the lengthening of life expectancy, more and more people are concerned with the effects of aging on their mental faculties (e.g., memory decline) and with the possibility of getting Alzheimer's Disease (AD) or other forms of dementia. This increasing awareness of AD has already resulted in a growing demand for neuropsychological testing. AD's research also emphasizes the need for early screening to improve the prediction of the disease progression and the efficacy of any future therapy. Such a drive to screen for pre-dementia raises the challenging issue of frontline identification of individuals in the preclinical or early clinical stages of AD. Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) is typically considered to be the prodromal state of AD, and is therefore at the core of the drive for early screening. Moreover, Pre-MCI so called SCI (Subjective Cognitive Impairment) can precede AD for 15 years. However, many individuals diagnosed with MCI do not convert to AD, some remaining stable and others even reversing back to normal (with rates of reversion to normal
chunks.title: Aging Stereotypes and Prodromal Alzheimer's Disease

chunks.text: individuals diagnosed with MCI do not convert to AD, some remaining stable and others even reversing back to normal (with rates of reversion to normal varying from 4.5% to as high as 53%). This over-diagnosis bias, which has been largely overlooked, is at the core of the present project at the interface of human and life sciences. Here, we argue that an important source of overdiagnosis in the prodromal state of AD comes from negative aging stereotypes (e.g., the culturally shared beliefs that aging inescapably causes severe cognitive decline and diseases such as AD) that permeate neuropsychological screening. There is ample evidence in the laboratory that such stereotypes contribute to the differences observed in the healthy population between younger and older adults in explicit memory tasks. Additionally, three pilot (lab) studies specifically conducted for the present ANR project showed that the threat of being judged stereotypically undermines the controlled use of memory of healthy older adults and simultaneously intensifies their automatic response tendencies, resulting in impaired memory performance. The present proposal goes several steps further by examining for the
chunks.title: Aging Stereotypes and Prodromal Alzheimer's Disease

chunks.text: es their automatic response tendencies, resulting in impaired memory performance. The present proposal goes several steps further by examining for the first time whether aging stereotypes are powerful enough to implicitly permeate the clinical neuropsychological testing and thus inflate memory deficits in older adults judged "at risk" (based on either epidemiological criteria or memory complaints), resulting in false-positive detection of SCI and MCI. This provocative hypothesis will be tested while 1) using biomarkers of neurodegeneration to distinguish false-positives from true MCI, and 2) using biomarkers of stress to examine whether and how aging stereotypes can lead to acute physiological stress during neuropsychological testing. This innovative project has the potential to offer new recommendations to improve the diagnosis accuracy of prodromal state of AD, with positive consequences for older people's wellbeing.

chunks.text:
Intervention: Life Skills and Resilience Program (BEHAVIORAL). The 12 week life skills course includes resiliency modules that complement the strengths of participants as they progress toward the development and achievement of personal goals. The first module of the intervention engages youth through a caring/supportive relationship that sets these expectations. Activities are designed to support youth in identifying their existing strengths/skills. The second module explores, with youth, how they can apply and build upon their strengths/skills in the pursuit of self-generated goals. The third module is dedicated to building upon key problem solving skills that are especially important for young adults with autism, including conflict resolution and the management of stressors. The fourth module builds leadership capacity and self-advocacy skills.
Study arm: Resilience Training (EXPERIMENTAL). This group will participate in the 12 week Life Skills and Resilience Program that includes vocational skills and adult skills important for an adult in society. Participants will also receive standard case management plus resiliency-focused support to encourage family and young adult

Participants will also receive standard case management plus resiliency-focused support to encourage family and young adult interaction with professionals and peers. chunks.text:
Intervention: Cognitive-Behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) (BEHAVIORAL). Participants with chronic primary insomnia are randomized into 2 groups with a 1:1 allocation ratio, after the completion of the pre-treatment assessment. Post-treatment and post-waitlist assessment occur after the 3-month treatment or waiting period.

One group will receive the intervention immediately after the pre-treatment assessment and the other group will receive the intervention after a waiting period of 3 months. The intervention consists of manualized cognitive-behavioural therapy for insomnia. This treatment includes psychoeducation about sleep and circadian rhythms, stimulus control, sleep restriction, relaxation, and cognitive therapy. The therapy is administered individually. Participants meet for 8 sessions of 50 minutes spread over 12 weeks.
Study arm: Immediate intervention (EXPERIMENTAL). 
Study arm: Waitlist (NO_INTERVENTION).
