Title: Psychotherapy for Irritability in Youth: Comparing Active Treatment to Nonactive Psychoeducation Supportive Psychotherapy
Conditions: Irritability, Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder, Oppositional Defiant Disorder, Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder
Brief summary: Background:

Irritability is defined as proneness to anger that may impair a person's ability to function. It is a common reason for why some children need mental health care. Yet no therapies have been developed just to target irritability. Researchers want to compare different types of therapy for irritability.

Objective:

To test different types of therapy for children and teens with severe irritability.

Eligibility:

People aged 8 to 16.5 years with severe irritability. Their parents are also needed.

Design:

Participants will have 28 study visits in 18 months.

They will have a baseline visit. They will answer questions about their mood, behavior, and daily life.

All parents and children will have 12 therapy sessions. Sessions will be once a week; they will last 30 to 60 minutes. Some of the child sessions may be done by telehealth.

Each parent and child will have 1 of 3 therapy
chunks.title: Psychotherapy for Irritability in Youth: Comparing Active Treatment to Nonactive Psychoeducation Supportive Psychotherapy

chunks.text:
be once a week; they will last 30 to 60 minutes. Some of the child sessions may be done by telehealth.

Each parent and child will have 1 of 3 therapy types:

Exposure therapy (child). Participants will face things that make them angry. A therapist will help them practice managing their anger.

Management therapy (parent). Therapists will coach parents on ways to manage their child s behaviors.

Psychoeducation/supportive psychotherapy (child and/or parent). Participants will talk with therapists about their or their child s feelings and behaviors. They will list their problems and goals; build coping skills; learn to relax; improve communication; and work on managing stress.

Sessions may be videotaped. Participants may opt out of being recorded.

Participants will have phone calls every 2 weeks during therapy. They will answer questions about how they are doing. Follow-up calls will continue for 1 year after therapy.

Title: The BANYAN Trial, an ALS MyMatch Trial Evaluating Safety, Biomarker Activity, and Microglial Activation of Nasal Foralumab
Conditions: ALS (Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis), ALS - Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis, ALS
Brief summary: The goal of this clinical trial is to learn whether a nasal spray medicine called foralumab is safe and easy to tolerate in adults with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). ALS is a disease that slowly damages the nerve cells that control movement, causing muscles to grow weaker over time. Foralumab is being studied as a possible way to calm the inflammation and immune system activity that are thought to play a role in ALS.

The main questions it aims to answer are:

1. Is nasal foralumab safe for people with ALS, and how well do they tolerate it over 12 and 24 weeks of treatment?
2. Does foralumab change certain markers in the blood and spinal fluid, and lower inflammation in the brain, compared with a placebo?

Researchers will compare people who take foralumab to people who take a placebo (a matching nasal spray with no medicine in it) to see how the two groups differ in safety and in these markers.

About 44 adults aged 18 to 75 with ALS will
chunks.title: The BANYAN Trial, an ALS MyMatch Trial Evaluating Safety, Biomarker Activity, and Microglial Activation of Nasal Foralumab

chunks.text:
hing nasal spray with no medicine in it) to see how the two groups differ in safety and in these markers.

About 44 adults aged 18 to 75 with ALS will take part. For the first 12 weeks, participants will be randomly assigned so that about 3 in 4 use foralumab and about 1 in 4 use the placebo. Neither the participants nor the study staff will know who is using which during this time (this is called "double-blind"). After the first 12 weeks, everyone who continues will use foralumab for the next 12 weeks.

Participants will:

* Spray the study treatment into both nostrils 3 times a week, on alternate days, in cycles of 2 weeks on treatment followed by 1 week off
* Learn to use the nasal spray device so they or a caregiver can give most doses at home
* Take part for about 8.5 months in total, which includes screening, 24 weeks of treatment, and a safety check-in about 4 weeks after the last dose
* Attend some visits at the study clinic and complete others remotely by phone or video
* Have study tests that may include blood samples, breathing and muscle-strength checks, and - for those who agree and at certain study centers - spinal fluid samples and brain scans to measure inflammation

chunks.text:
Title: OPM- MEG in Non-immune And iMmune-medIated Neurological Disease
Conditions: Autoimmune Encephalitis (AE), Acute Disseminated Encephalomyelitis, Multiple Sclerosis
Brief summary: Over the past 20 years, doctors have gotten much better at spotting and treating brain conditions caused by the immune system attacking the body. These include illnesses like autoimmune encephalitis, ADEM, and multiple sclerosis. But even with better treatments, many patients-especially children-still struggle with long-term problems. Standard brain scans and tests often miss important issues like memory problems, emotional difficulties, trouble sleeping, and challenges with social behaviour. Early research using a special brain imaging technique (called MEG) has shown changes in brain networks that seem to be linked to poor memory. This study will use a new, advanced version of MEG that works even with very young children (as young as 2 years old). The goal is to better understand how these brain conditions affect children, compare them with other types of brain illness, and eventually use this technology to help predict outcomes and discover new ways to track brain health.

Title: Neuroplasticity Enhancement From Cognitive Training Reinforced by Psilocybin
Conditions: Alzheimer's Disease
Brief summary: Background:

Normal aging, as well as dementias such as Alzheimer s disease, can cause changes in the brain that affect memory, attention, and thinking. Researchers want to know if regular mental tasks (cognitive training) can improve brain function in older adults. They also want to know if psilocybin, a compound found in certain mushrooms, can further support improved brain function.

Objective:

To learn how regular cognitive training, with or without psilocybin, can improve brain health in older adults.

Eligibility:

People aged 65 years and older with mild cognitive impairment or early-stage Alzheimer s disease. Healthy older adults with normal cognition are also needed.

Design:

Participants will be screened. They will have a test of their heart function and an imaging scan. They will have mental health screening and tests of their thinking and memory. They will practice brain-training tasks on a tablet.

Participants will be divided into 2 groups: 1 will have cognitive training plus psilocybin; 1 will have cognitive training only.

Those
chunks.title: Neuroplasticity Enhancement From Cognitive Training Reinforced by Psilocybin

chunks.text:
on a tablet.

Participants will be divided into 2 groups: 1 will have cognitive training plus psilocybin; 1 will have cognitive training only.

Those having cognitive training only will have 5 or 6 clinic visits. They will take the tablet home to practice brain training daily. They will wear a device to measure brain waves as they sleep; they may have 1 overnight stay in the clinic, or they may wear the device at home. Imaging scans and other tests will be repeated at each visit.

Those taking psilocybin will have up to 9 clinic visits. In addition to the visits for cognitive training, they will take 1 psilocybin capsule by mouth 2 weeks apart (the second dose is optional). They will remain in the clinic for 24 hours after each dose.

Conditions: Stroke, Stroke (6 Months or More After Onset)
Brief summary: Stroke survivors often experience persistent unmet needs during long-term recovery. Young and middle-aged stroke survivors may face additional challenges in balancing rehabilitation with work and family responsibilities. Although digital health interventions have the potential to improve access to education and self-management support, existing programs are often provider-driven, provide limited peer support, and have short follow-up periods.

This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of a patient-centered digital education and peer support intervention co-designed with young and middle-aged stroke survivors. Participants will be randomly assigned to either the intervention group or the usual care group. The intervention will be delivered through LINE communities and Google collaborative platforms over a 12-month period. The primary outcome is unmet needs. Title: Tenecteplase or Reteplase as Bridging Thrombolysis Before Thrombectomy in Acute Ischemic Cerebrovascular Events
Conditions: Acute Ischemic Stroke, Large Vessel Occlusion, Anterior Circulation Brain Infarction
Brief summary: Acute ischemic stroke caused by large vessel occlusion (LVO) is a major cause of disability, and mechanical thrombectomy (MT) has become the standard treatment for eligible patients. However, the optimal role of intravenous thrombolysis before MT remains uncertain.

The TRACE-BRIDGE trial is a phase 3, investigator-initiated, multicenter, randomized, open-label trial with blinded outcome assessment (PROBE design) evaluating different bridging thrombolysis strategies before MT. The trial will enroll adults with acute ischemic stroke presenting within 4.5 hours of symptom onset and with imaging-confirmed anterior circulation LVO who are eligible for intravenous thrombolysis and MT.

Participants will be randomly assigned in a 1:1:1 ratio to receive tenecteplase plus MT, reteplase plus MT, or direct MT alone. The TRACE-BRIDGE trial aims to evaluate the efficacy and safety of bridging thrombolysis with tenecteplase or reteplase before mechanical thrombectomy
chunks.title: Tenecteplase or Reteplase as Bridging Thrombolysis Before Thrombectomy in Acute Ischemic Cerebrovascular Events

chunks.text: The TRACE-BRIDGE trial aims to evaluate the efficacy and safety of bridging thrombolysis with tenecteplase or reteplase before mechanical thrombectomy compared with direct mechanical thrombectomy. The primary outcome is functional independence, defined as a modified Rankin Scale score of 0-2 at 90 days after randomization. If superiority of bridging thrombolysis is demonstrated, the trial will further evaluate whether reteplase is non-inferior to tenecteplase as a bridging thrombolytic strategy.

Title: Augmenting Parent Management Training for Child Temper Outbursts Using a Digital Tool
Conditions: Disruptive Behavior Disorders, Conduct Disorder, Oppositional Defiant Disorder, Attention-deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder
Brief summary: Background:

Pediatric disruptive behavior disorders (DBDs) are characterized by severe irritability, anger, and temper outbursts. The primary way to treat children with DBDs is parent management training (PMT). PMT teaches parents how to reward desired behaviors and not to reward undesired ones. Researchers want to find out if a smartphone app can help parents apply these skills more effectively.

Objective:

To test a smartphone app to enhance PMT.

Eligibility:

Children aged 8 to 13 years with DBDs. A parent or guardian is also needed.

Design:

Parents will have 12 weekly sessions of PMT. PMT teaches them how to manage their child s mood and behaviors. Parents will learn to actively ignore, praise, set limits, and handle temper outbursts. PMT can be either in person or via video. Sessions last 30 to 60 minutes. They will be video and audio recorded.

Parents will be divided into 2 groups. Only 1 group will download a smartphone app. The
chunks.title: Augmenting Parent Management Training for Child Temper Outbursts Using a Digital Tool

chunks.text:
last 30 to 60 minutes. They will be video and audio recorded.

Parents will be divided into 2 groups. Only 1 group will download a smartphone app. The app helps parents practice PMT skills. It offers videos, a resource library, and alerts when a child may be at risk for various behaviors.

All parents will be prompted every day to answer questions about their child s mood and their own behavior. These will continue until 12 weeks after their last PMT session.

Children will also answer questions on their phone daily for 1 week at a time. They will do this on 3 different weeks, each about 2 months apart. They will also have check-ins by phone every 2 weeks for up to 6 months.

Parents will have follow-up calls 3, 6, and 12 months after they finish PMT.

Brief summary: The goal of this controlled pre-post-trial is to test the Accu-Chek SmartGuide continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) system and whether its predictive features provide additional benefits for adults with type 1 diabetes or insulin- treated type 2 diabetes.

The main questions this study aims to answer are:

* Does using the Accu-Chek SmartGuide together with the Predict App change participants' fear of hypoglycemia?

diabetes empowerment?

Conditions: Parkinson Disease, Idiopathic
Brief summary: The aim of this pilot study is to assess whether an online Mediterranean diet programme called MediPD is acceptable and practical for people living with Parkinson's disease, and whether it can help them make and maintain changes towards a Mediterranean-style diet.

The study will include 120 adults living in the United Kingdom with Parkinson's disease who have access to an internet-enabled device and currently have low adherence to a Mediterranean-style diet. Participants will be randomly assigned to one of two groups. One group will receive access to the MediPD online programme, which includes short educational videos, personalised dietary information, practical resources, goal-setting tools, and online dietetic support. The other group will continue with their usual care and will receive access to MediPD after completing the final study assessment.

Researchers will compare the groups to see whether MediPD improves adherence to a Mediterranean diet after 24 weeks. The study will also examine dietary intake, non-motor symptoms,

By being more informed, patients can discuss their wishes with their family members or future caregivers, include preferences in advanced directives, and/or have a discussion with their medical provider about their future care preferences.
Study arm: The Choose Your Own Adventure Patient Journey with Dementia booklet (CYOA booklet) (OTHER).

Primary outcome: The Dementia Knowledge Assessment Tool (DKAT2)
Time frame: Participants will complete the DKAT2 at baseline, and 1-30 days after reviewing the toolkit at follow-up telephone encounter. The follow-up assessment window may extend 30 additional days if participants wish to remain in the study.
Dementia knowledge will be assessed using the 21-item Dementia Knowledge Assessment Tool Version 2 (DKAT2), which was developed to assess foundation-level knowledge of dementia. Each item has three response options: Yes, No, and Don't Know. Each correct response is assigned 1 point, while an incorrect or Don't Know response is assigned 0 points. Total scores range from 0 to 21, with higher scores indicating greater dementia knowledge.

The baseline and follow up assessment may be completed either independently using a paper questionnaire or as an interviewer-administered questionnaire by study personnel. The change in total DKAT2 score from baseline to post-intervention will be assessed.
Primary outcome: Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool (PEMAT)
Time frame: PEMAT will be completed 1-30 days after reviewing the toolkit at follow-up telephone encounter along with DKAT2.

Time frame: PEMAT will be completed 1-30 days after reviewing the toolkit at follow-up telephone encounter along with DKAT2. The follow-up assessment window may extend 30 additional days if participants wish to remain in the study.
Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool (PEMAT), will be used to assess understandability and actionability of print educational material. The PEMAT provides two domain scores: understandability and actionability. Understandability is assessed using 17 items, and actionability is assessed using 7 items. Each applicable item is scored as 1 (agree) or 0 (disagree). Domain scores are calculated as the percentage of applicable items receiving a score of 1. Scores range from 0% to 100% for each domain, with higher scores indicating greater understandability and actionability. Understandability and actionability scores will be reported separately. The PEMAT may be completed as an interviewer-administered questionnaire by study personnel.

chunks.text:
Title: A Study to Learn About the Safety of BIIB147 and Its Effects in Adults With Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS)
Conditions: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis
Brief summary: In this study, researchers will learn more about the effects of BIIB147, in participants with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, also known as ALS. ALS is a rare disease that damages the motor neurons in the brain and spinal cord that help control the movement of muscles in the body. It is a progressive disease, which means that it gets worse with time. Over time, this causes increasing problems with speaking, swallowing, moving the arms and legs, and breathing. In the case of ALS, this eventually leads to death from patients not being able to breathe.

This is a "first-in-human" study. This means that this study drug will be given to people for the very first time in this study. These studies are important because they help researchers learn about the safety of the study drug, how the body processes it, and what dose might be appropriate before testing it in larger groups.

The main goal of the study is to learn about the safety of BIIB147 in adult participants with ALS. The main question researchers want to
chunks.title: A Study to Learn About the Safety of BIIB147 and Its Effects in Adults With Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS)

chunks.text:
rger groups.

The main goal of the study is to learn about the safety of BIIB147 in adult participants with ALS. The main question researchers want to answer is:

* How many participants have adverse events and serious adverse events during the study? Adverse events are health problems that may or may not be caused by the study drug.
* Researchers will also learn more about:

  * How much BIIB147 gets into the blood?
  * What is the highest amount of BIIB147 found in the blood?
  * How long does it take BIIB147 to reach its highest amount in the blood?
  * How much neurofilament light chain (NfL) protein is found in the blood?
  * How longer-term treatment with BIIB147 affects disease worsening and the participants' overall survival?

This study will be done as follows:

* Participants will join the study after signing an informed consent form, also known as an ICF.
* Participants will be screened to check if they can join the study. The screening period will be up to 4 weeks.
* Participants will be randomly assigned to get either the study drug BIIB147 or a placebo during the main treatment period. A placebo is something that looks like the study drug but does not contain any
chunks.title: A Study to Learn About the Safety of BIIB147 and Its Effects in Adults With Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS)

chunks.text:
r the study drug BIIB147 or a placebo during the main treatment period. A placebo is something that looks like the study drug but does not contain any medicine. A placebo is also given the same as the study drug.
* Neither the participants nor the researchers will know if participants are getting the study drug or the placebo.
* BIIB147 or the placebo will be given through a lumbar puncture. This is done using a thin needle that is put into the lower part of the spine.
* During the main treatment period, participants will have regular clinic visits and phone calls. At the visits, the study doctor will do tests to check the participants' overall health, including their brain and nerve function. The participants' breathing function, tongue strength, and muscle strength will also be checked. They will also measure the participants' height, weight, and vital signs and collect blood and urine samples. Participants will also complete questionnaires or answer questions about how they are feeling and about their daily lives.
* After finishing treatment in the main part of the study, some participants who qualify may be able to join a "long-term extension" part of the study. This may last
chunks.title: A Study to Learn About the Safety of BIIB147 and Its Effects in Adults With Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS)

chunks.text:
ng treatment in the main part of the study, some participants who qualify may be able to join a "long-term extension" part of the study. This may last up to 6 years or more. During this part of the study, all participants will get BIIB147.
* After the long-term extension is done, participants will join a follow-up safety period. If participants do not enter the long-term extension, they will go directly into the follow-up safety period once the treatment period is done.
* Each participant will be in the study for up to 8 years or more.

Eligibility criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

1. Borderzone or superficial territorial ischemic stroke, or cortical TIA, within 30 days before enrollment, attributed to 70% to 100% atherosclerotic stenosis/occlusion of the intracranial ICA or the MCA (M1 or dominant/co-dominant M2). The eligible borderzone strokes are cortical (external) borderzone infarcts, located between the anterior and middle cerebral artery territories or between the middle and posterior cerebral artery territories; internal borderzone infarcts are not included. A cortical TIA is defined as transient cortical dysfunction evidenced by either visual field defects, spatial neglect, disorder of language, memory, or orientation. The corresponding cerebral artery atherosclerosis may be diagnosed by CTA, contrast-enhanced MRI, or catheter angiography.
2. Evidence of perfusion impairment (minimum: TMax delay ≥ 6 sec, vol ≥ 5 cc) in CTP or perfusion MRI.
3. Functional status better than severely disabled (mRS score 0-3).

chunks.text:
disabled (mRS score 0-3).

   * Insulin-dependent diabetes for at least 15 years.

chunks.text:
ease.

chunks.title: EDAS Revascularization for Symptomatic Intracranial Atherosclerotic Steno-occlusive Disease

chunks.text:
Intervention: Encephaloduroarteriosynangiosis (EDAS) (PROCEDURE). EDAS is a form of indirect revascularization for cerebral arterial steno-occlusive disorders. The superficial temporal artery (STA) is dissected from the scalp, while maintaining its proximal and terminal connections to the external carotid artery and the skin tissues. The STA is then rerouted under the skull and placed in close proximity to the cortical branches of the middle cerebral artery without a direct anastomosis. EDAS is performed no later than 7 days after randomization.
Intervention: Intensive medical management (OTHER). Medical management administered to both study arms following current and updated standard-of-care parameters, with guidance and oversight from the trial's Medical Management Core. Antiplatelet treatment with aspirin for the entire follow-up and dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin plus a P2Y12 receptor inhibitor for up to 90 days after randomization; management of the primary risk factors targeting systolic blood pressure \<140 mmHg and LDL \<70 mg/dL; management of the secondary risk factors (diabetes, non-HDL cholesterol, smoking, weight, physical activity) with the assistance of a
chunks.title: EDAS Revascularization for Symptomatic Intracranial Atherosclerotic Steno-occlusive Disease

chunks.text:
LDL \<70 mg/dL; management of the secondary risk factors (diabetes, non-HDL cholesterol, smoking, weight, physical activity) with the assistance of a lifestyle modification program. The management protocol may be modified during the trial to reflect the most up-to-date, evidence-based practices; changes apply to participants in both groups.
Study arm: EDAS plus intensive medical management (EXPERIMENTAL). EDAS performed no later than 7 days after randomization, plus intensive medical management. Participants in this group receive aspirin without interruption and do not receive a P2Y12 inhibitor from 5 days before until 7 days after surgery.
Study arm: Intensive medical management alone (ACTIVE_COMPARATOR). Intensive medical management following current guidelines for the management of patients with symptomatic intracranial atherosclerotic disease.
chunks.title: EDAS Revascularization for Symptomatic Intracranial Atherosclerotic Steno-occlusive Disease

chunks.text:
Primary outcome: Rate of any stroke or death within 30 days of randomization, or ischemic stroke in the territory of the qualifying artery thereafter
Time frame: From randomization through the end of follow-up (minimum 18 months, maximum 54 months, mean 30 months)
The composite of any stroke (ischemic or hemorrhagic) or death within 30 days of randomization plus recurrent ischemic stroke in the territory of the qualifying artery thereafter during full follow-up. Possible events are centrally adjudicated; the outcome measure is the centrally adjudicated, blinded event, not the site-determined event. Cumulative event rates in the two groups are compared by Kaplan-Meier estimates at 2.5 years.

chunks.text:
Title: EDAS Revascularization for Symptomatic Intracranial Atherosclerotic Steno-occlusive Disease
Conditions: Intracranial Atherosclerosis, Intracranial Arterial Stenosis, Ischemic Stroke
Brief summary: ERSIAS IIb is a multicenter randomized controlled trial, with a Phase IIb design, to find out whether encephaloduroarteriosynangiosis (EDAS), a type of indirect surgical revascularization of the brain, added to intensive medical management, lowers the rate of recurrent stroke and death compared with intensive medical management alone. The trial enrolls 170 adults who have had a recent ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack caused by intracranial atherosclerotic disease, with a narrowing or blockage of at least 70% of the intracranial internal carotid artery or the middle cerebral artery and reduced blood flow in the territory of that artery. Participants are assigned at random, in equal numbers, to EDAS plus intensive medical management or to intensive medical management alone, and are followed for 18 to 54 months.

chunks.text:
Intervention: BELL-001 Digital Therapeutic (DEVICE). Smartphone-based digital therapeutic that plays sound linked to the user's breathing phase through insert earphones. In this study, the participant's own touchscreen press (inhalation) and release (exhalation) served as the breathing-phase signal during the active stage, followed by a sound sequence that slowed from the breathing rate established in the active stage. A respiration belt was used for recording only and was not an input to the application.
Intervention: Sham Digital Therapeutic (DEVICE). Application with the same appearance and screen flow as BELL-001 that plays a single fixed pre-recorded sound not linked to breathing, with brief tones at random intervals during the active stage to match the touch task.
Study arm: BELL-001 (EXPERIMENTAL). Participants used the BELL-001 smartphone application during one laboratory visit, with sound delivered through insert earphones. After a short practice, a brief auditory evoked potential recording and 10 minutes of eyes-closed rest, participants completed a 10-minute active stage in which they held the touchscreen pressed during each inhalation and released it during each
chunks.title: Brain and Heart Rhythm Responses to a Breathing-Linked Sound Application (BELL-001) in Adults With Insomnia Symptoms

chunks.text:
ed rest, participants completed a 10-minute active stage in which they held the touchscreen pressed during each inhalation and released it during each exhalation while the application played sounds that followed this press-and-release signal, and then a 50-minute passive listening stage in which the pace of the sound slowed gradually from the breathing rate established in the active stage. Eyes remained closed throughout the recording. After the visit, participants used BELL-001 at home for 7 nights in an open-label period, as did participants in the sham group.
Study arm: Sham (SHAM_COMPARATOR). Participants used a sham application with the same appearance and screen flow during one laboratory visit, with the same practice, auditory evoked potential recording and 10 minutes of eyes-closed rest. During the 10-minute active stage, they tapped the touchscreen each time they heard a brief tone presented at random intervals of 2 to 12 seconds. During the 50-minute passive stage, a single fixed pre-recorded sound that was not linked to breathing was played. Eyes remained closed throughout the recording. After the visit, participants in this group also used the BELL-001 application (not
chunks.title: Brain and Heart Rhythm Responses to a Breathing-Linked Sound Application (BELL-001) in Adults With Insomnia Symptoms

chunks.text:
Title: Brain and Heart Rhythm Responses to a Breathing-Linked Sound Application (BELL-001) in Adults With Insomnia Symptoms
Conditions: Insomnia
Brief summary: The purpose of this study was to describe how brain activity and heart rhythm respond to BELL-001, a smartphone application that plays sounds linked to the user's own breathing, compared with a sham application that looks the same but does not link its sounds to breathing. Adults with self-reported insomnia symptoms were randomly assigned to BELL-001 or to the sham application. During one laboratory visit, brain activity was recorded with electroencephalography (EEG), heart activity with electrocardiography (ECG), and breathing with a chest belt while participants rested with their eyes closed, then used the assigned application actively for 10 minutes, and then listened passively for 50 minutes. After the visit, all participants, regardless of laboratory group, used the BELL-001 application at home for 7 nights in an open-label period while wearing a smartwatch.

Brief summary: Researchers at OpenMindXR, in collaboration with Indiana University, are conducting a paid research study evaluating an innovative virtual reality (VR)-based intervention designed to support social and emotional skill development in children and adolescents with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). Children with ADHD often experience challenges in social functioning, emotional regulation, and peer relationships. Title: Cognitive Effects of Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy (HBOT) After a Traumatic Brain Injury
Conditions: Adults Who Sustained a Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI), Adults Who Treated With a Course of Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy
Brief summary: This is a retrospective, single-center observational study evaluating the cognitive effects of hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) in adults who sustained a traumatic brain injury (TBI). Earlier randomized controlled work at this center demonstrated cognitive improvement after HBOT in patients with chronic deficits following mild TBI. This study evaluates a large sample size and operationalizes HBOT treatment as a continuous variable in the form of a cumulative oxygen dose, something has not been done before. Using the medical records of patients treated at the Sagol Center for Hyperbaric Medicine and Research at Shamir Medical Center between 2008 and 2026, the investigators compare computerized NeuroTrax cognitive assessments obtained before and after HBOT. The investigators quantify within-patient change across the cognitive domains and the Global Cognitive Score, and test whether the magnitude of cognitive change is associated with cumulative oxygen

Brief summary: LEOPARD is a multicenter study aimed at improving the genetic diagnosis of patients with neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) of unknown etiology, particularly those with moderate-to-severe intellectual disability. The study combines reanalysis of previously generated genetic data with additional molecular investigations, including functional validation of variants of uncertain significance, RNA sequencing, and DNA methylation profiling. The project also aims to develop a computational infrastructure to support data reanalysis, integration, storage, and sharing, thereby improving the diagnostic workflow for rare diseases and supporting personalized patient care.

Study arm: Older Adults with Mild Cognitive Impairment (). Older adults aged 65 years or older undergoing elective major orthopedic or complex spine surgery who meet protocol-defined psychometric criteria for mild cognitive impairment. Study arm: Cognitively Intact Older Adults (). Older adults aged 65 years or older undergoing elective major orthopedic or complex spine surgery who do not meet criteria for mild cognitive impairment. Participants undergo the same longitudinal assessments as the MCI cohort.

Primary outcome: Past 24-Hour Average Pain Intensity
Time frame: Baseline, 2 weeks, 1 month, 3 months, and 6 months after surgery.
Average postoperative pain intensity will be measured using an 11-point Numeric Rating Scale (NRS) ranging from 0 (No Pain) to 10 (Worst Possible Pain). Participants will rate their average pain during the previous 24 hours at each assessment. Title: Postsurgical Pain and Opioid Use in Older Adults: Effects of Mild Cognitive Impairment
Conditions: Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI), Opioid Use, Cognitive Dysfunction, Postoperative Pain
Brief summary: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) affects a substantial proportion of older adults undergoing major surgery and may alter pain processing, pain experience, and opioid use after surgery. This prospective observational cohort study will compare older adults with MCI and cognitively intact older adults undergoing major orthopedic and complex spine procedures. Participants will undergo preoperative assessment of cognitive function, quantitative sensory testing, heart rate variability, clinical pain, and biomarkers associated with Alzheimer's disease risk. Postoperative pain trajectories, opioid use, pain responsiveness, and cognitive outcomes will be evaluated for six months following surgery. The study aims to determine whether MCI is associated with differences in postoperative pain and opioid use outcomes and whether APOE4 status and plasma amyloid beta 42/40 ratio contribute to observed differences.

chunks.text:
Title: Prospective Longitudinal Study of Sleep, Brain Activity, and Plasma Analyses in Patients Undergoing Epilepsy Surgery
Conditions: Epilepsy, Sleep, Drug Resistant Epilepsy, Epilepsy Sleep, Surgery
Brief summary: The goal of this observational study is to understand how sleep and brain activity change after epilepsy surgery in adults with drug-resistant epilepsy. Drug-resistant epilepsy means that seizures continue despite treatment with appropriate medications.

The study will investigate whether changes in sleep and brain activity are related to seizure control, sleep quality, and quality of life after surgery.

The main questions it aims to answer are:

* How do sleep patterns and brain activity change after epilepsy surgery?
* How are changes in sleep and brain activity related to seizure control and quality of life?
* Do sleep patterns after surgery become more like those of healthy adults?
* How are changes in blood proteins related to sleep, brain activity, and seizure control? Researchers will follow 30 adults undergoing epilepsy surgery. Their sleep will be compared with that of 10 healthy adults of similar age and sex. Healthy participants will complete the study
chunks.title: Prospective Longitudinal Study of Sleep, Brain Activity, and Plasma Analyses in Patients Undergoing Epilepsy Surgery

chunks.text:
ing epilepsy surgery. Their sleep will be compared with that of 10 healthy adults of similar age and sex. Healthy participants will complete the study assessments once.

Participants undergoing epilepsy surgery will complete the assessments before surgery and approximately 2 and 6 months after surgery.

At each assessment, participants will:

* Wear a small device (actigraph) on their wrist for about 2 weeks to measure sleep and activity and keep a sleep diary.
* Spend 2 consecutive nights at a patient hotel while their sleep and brain activity are recorded using polysomnography (PSG), a test that measures sleep, breathing, and brain activity.
* Answer questionnaires about sleep quality, insomnia, mood, and quality of life.
* Provide blood samples for research. Researchers will also collect information about seizure frequency, medications, and medical history.

The sleep recordings will be used to study several aspects of sleep, including:

* Sleep architecture: how much time participants spend in different stages of sleep and how often their sleep is interrupted.
* Sleep spindles and slow oscillations: patterns of brain activity during sleep that are involved in how the brain
chunks.title: Prospective Longitudinal Study of Sleep, Brain Activity, and Plasma Analyses in Patients Undergoing Epilepsy Surgery

chunks.text:
w often their sleep is interrupted.
* Sleep spindles and slow oscillations: patterns of brain activity during sleep that are involved in how the brain processes and organizes information.
* Cyclic alternating pattern (CAP): a measure of brief changes in brain activity during sleep that can provide information about sleep stability.
* Epileptiform activity: abnormal electrical activity in the brain that may be associated with epilepsy and can occur during sleep.

Researchers will also analyze proteins in blood samples to explore whether biological changes are related to sleep and seizure outcomes.

Epilepsy surgery and other medical treatments will be decided by the participants' treating healthcare teams, independently of this study. The study will observe changes before and after surgery without assigning participants to a treatment.

Intervention: Sleep MAPP Care Pathway (OTHER). The Sleep MAPP Care Pathway includes four components: (1) the Sleep MAPP clinical decision-support tool, which identifies Veterans who may benefit from insomnia screening and provides clinicians with screening results and care prompts; (2) insomnia screening using the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI); (3) training PNS rehabilitation clinicians to deliver Brief Behavioral Treatment for Insomnia (BBTI); and (4) delivery of BBTI to clinically appropriate Veterans as part of routine care. BBTI is a brief, evidence-based behavioral treatment for insomnia that includes sleep education, stimulus control, sleep restriction, and strategies to support adherence and maintenance of treatment gains.
Study arm: Sleep MAPP Care Pathway (EXPERIMENTAL). The participating Polytrauma/TBI System of Care clinic will implement the Sleep MAPP Care Pathway, which is designed to increase delivery of two guideline-recommended clinical practices: insomnia screening with the Insomnia Severity Index and Brief Behavioral Treatment for Insomnia (BBTI). Implementation will be supported by a multicomponent strategy bundle that includes deployment of the Sleep MAPP

Title: Sleep MAPP in the Polytrauma/TBI System of Care
Conditions: Insomnia Disorder, Mild Traumatic Brain Injury
Brief summary: This pilot implementation trial will evaluate the Sleep Disorder Management Assistance for Providers and Patients (Sleep MAPP) Care Pathway in one Veterans Health Administration Polytrauma/TBI System of Care clinic. The care pathway combines a provider-facing decision-support tool that supports pre-visit administration and documentation of the Insomnia Severity Index with training and implementation support for clinic providers to deliver Brief Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia. The study will assess the feasibility and acceptability of the care pathway; describe changes in guideline-concordant insomnia screening and behavioral treatment; and describe preliminary changes in insomnia symptoms, neurobehavioral symptoms, and participation in social roles among Veterans with mild traumatic brain injury who receive Brief Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia. Up to 30 clinic providers or staff and 50 Veterans will be invited to complete research surveys and interviews. Implementation and clinical outcomes will be obtained from routinely collected clinical data.

Primary outcome: Movement Disorder Society Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS): Parts I, II, and IV
Time frame: Day 1
The MDS-UPDRS is a standardized clinical assessment used by neurologists to study PD. Three parts (I/II/IV) are used to evaluate individuals' symptoms of Parkinson's Disease, including non-motor and motor experiences of daily living and common PD comorbidities. Each part contains several items (each rated by severity on a 0 to 4 scale) Part I (subscale from 0-52), Part II (subscale from 0-52), and Part IV (subscale from 0-24) are summed for a total score from 0-128. A higher score indicates higher severity of PD-related symptoms.
Primary outcome: REM Behavioral Disorder Screening Questionnaire (RBDSQ)
Time frame: Day 1
RBDSQ is a simple 10-item yes/no response screening questionnaire to screen for REM sleep behavior disorders, a known risk factor for PD. The range for this scale is 0 to 13 points. Each item contributes 1 point except a single item that contributes 4 points for up to four specific manifestations of REM Behavior Disorders. A score of 5 or higher indicates a positive screening threshold for REM Behavioral Disorder (RBD).

Primary outcome: Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA)
Time frame: Day 1
MoCA is a 10-minute cognitive screening tool used to detect mild-cognitive impairment (MCI) by assessing short-term memory, visuospatial abilities, executive functions, attention and concentration, working memory, language, and orientation to time and place. The scale ranges from 0 to 30 points. Severe impairment scores between 0-9 and normal cognitive performance scored at 26 and above. The higher the score, the less cognitive impairment.
Primary outcome: Scales for Outcomes in Parkinson's Disease - Autonomic Dysfunction (SCOPA-AUT)
Time frame: Day 1
SCOPA-AUT is a 25-item questionnaire used to assess autonomic symptoms (gastrointestinal, urinary, cardiovascular, thermoregulatory, pupillomotor, sexual) in patients with Parkinson's disease. This scale includes subscales for gastrointestinal (0-7), urinary (0-6), cardiovascular (0-3), thermoregulatory (0-4), pupillomotor (0-1), and sexual (2 items for men and 2 items for women) symptoms. Total scale ranges from 0-23

Primary outcome: University of Pennsylvania Smell Identification Test (UPSIT)
Time frame: Day 1
UPSIT is a reliable 40-item test of olfactory function using microencapsulated odorants which are released by scratching scent strips across four small booklets. The individual then picks the answer from a list of four multiple-choice options. The final score is the number of correct answers between 0 and 40. A lower score indicates olfactory dysfunction, and a higher score indicates a more normal sense of smell.

chunks.text:
Title: Parkinson's Disease in Type 1 Gaucher Disease
Conditions: Parkinson Disease (PD), Type 1 Gaucher Disease
Brief summary: Parkinson's disease (PD) is an age-related movement disorder with a complex pathophysiology. Among the risk factors for PD, variants in beta-glucocerebrosidase (encoded by the gene GBA1) represent one of the most significant heritable risk factors for lifetime PD risk. Biallelic variants in GBA1 cause Gaucher disease (GD), a multisystem disorder, and individuals with late/adult-onset GD1 have a \~1-in-9 lifetime risk for PD. This study aims to develop a cross-sectional cohort of clinical and laboratory phenotyped adult GD1 patients and controls for investigation of clinical/laboratory risk factors for current and future Parkinson risk. Neurological evaluations will be video and audio recorded to allow the investigators to quantify neurological function using automated tools. Data and specimens generated in this study will be incorporated into a de-identified biobank that will be used for further research into GD and PD.

Title: Adapting the Sensory Environment to Reduce Stress in Children With Autism During Dental Visits
Conditions: Autism, Autism Disorders and Maternal Stress, Sensory Integration Disorder, Stress Biomarkers
Brief summary: This study aims to evaluate the impact of a sensory-adapted dental environment (SADE) on the stress levels and behavioral responses of children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) during dental visits.

Children with ASD often experience sensory sensitivities, making traditional dental care challenging and stressful. In this study, 40 children aged 8 to 12 diagnosed with ASD, along with their parents or legal guardians, will participate in two standard dental visits spaced 30 days apart. The first visit will take place under standard clinical conditions, while the second visit will utilize a sensory-adapted dental environment featuring modified visual elements (such as dark protective glasses), auditory (noise-canceling headphones or relaxing music), taste (unflavored toothpaste), smell (sweet orange essential oil) and tactile adjustments (a weighted blanket).

The study will measure stress using objective tools, including continuous digital biomarkers of stress
chunks.title: Adapting the Sensory Environment to Reduce Stress in Children With Autism During Dental Visits

chunks.text:
and tactile adjustments (a weighted blanket).

The study will measure stress using objective tools, including continuous digital biomarkers of stress recorded via wristbands (such as heart rate, electrodermal activity, accelerometer data, actigraphy, movement intensity, step count, metabolic equivalent of task, skin temperature, and peripheral body orientation) and the analysis of salivary lysozyme and cortisol levels in both children and parents. Additionally, standardized psychological questionnaires will be used to assess the child's sensory profile, as well as parental stress and coping strategies. The findings will help determine whether modifying the sensory environment can effectively reduce anxiety and improve the dental care experience for children with autism.

Brief summary: This trial is a 12-month safety and feasibility study, enrolling up to six participants. These participants will serve as their own controls, structured in multiple parts that follow an initial short-term stereo electroencephalography (SEEG) mapping period.

During this trial we aim to demonstrate the safety of acute and chronic network-guided stimulation in Mild Cognitive Impairment by evaluating adverse effects, tolerability, and feasibility during both the short- term SEEG mapping phase and subsequent permanent DBS therapy.

In addition to safety measures, therapeutic results as follows are to be tested for: (1) Develop patient-specific stimulation parameters for the treatment of MCI, as well as develop and test memory state classifiers by enrolling six individuals to undergo intracranial mapping (SEEG). We will use targeted memory tasks to generate neural data needed for state distinctions, and conduct a
chunks.title: Deep Brain Stimulation Guided by Brain Mapping to Treat Cognitive Impairment

viduals to undergo intracranial mapping (SEEG). We will use targeted memory tasks to generate neural data needed for state distinctions, and conduct a systematic parameter search to identify and develop optimal settings for each patient. (2) Assess efficacy of open loop stimulation by delivering a fixed open loop protocol based on the parameters discovered earlier, while SEEG electrodes remain in place, and testing the efficacy of the trained classifier to detect favorable brain states. (3) Evaluate chronic DBS therapy by implanting a permanent system in participants who show an acute beneficial response to assess long term outcomes. (4) Assess therapeutic outcomes and refine protocols by measuring reductions in memory-related impairment.

The above findings will guide further refinement of the device and protocol.

Intervention: Multimodal Rehabilitation Program (BEHAVIORAL). Participants received a supervised multimodal rehabilitation program twice weekly for 12 weeks (24 sessions). The program included approximately 10 minutes of warm-up exercises, 20 minutes of progressive balance training, and 20 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise using a treadmill or stationary bicycle. Balance exercises included static and dynamic balance tasks, multidirectional stepping, functional mobility activities, turning, and dual-task training. Additional balance training was performed using the Korebalance Premiere-19 system. Exercise intensity was generally maintained at a Borg Rating of Perceived Exertion of 11-14. Exercises were individually progressed according to participant ability and safety.
Study arm: Multimodal Rehabilitation Group (EXPERIMENTAL). Participants with Parkinson's disease received a 12-week supervised multimodal rehabilitation program, conducted twice weekly. The intervention included progressive balance exercises, functional mobility training, dual-task activities, moderate-intensity aerobic exercise, and Korebalance-assisted balance training. All participants received the

chunks.text:
Title: Multimodal Rehabilitation and Balance Assessment in Parkinson's Disease
Conditions: Parkinson Disease (PD)
Brief summary: This study aimed to investigate the relationship between instrumented balance measurements and clinical balance assessments in individuals with Parkinson's disease and to evaluate changes in balance and functional mobility following a 12-week multimodal rehabilitation program.

Eighteen individuals with Parkinson's disease participated in this prospective, single-group study. All participants received a rehabilitation program that included balance exercises, aerobic exercise, and balance training using the Korebalance system. The program was conducted twice weekly for 12 weeks.

Balance was assessed using the Korebalance system and the Berg Balance Scale (BBS). Functional mobility was evaluated using the Timed Up and Go (TUG) test. Assessments were performed before and after the rehabilitation program.

The study examined whether instrumented balance measurements were associated with clinical balance performance and whether balance and functional mobility changed following rehabilitation.

Title: Study of the Link Between Structural Alterations in the Hypothalamus and Cardiac Dysautonomia in Drug-resistant Epilepsy
Conditions: Epilepsy, Hypothalamus, Seizures- Cardiac Dysautonomia, SUDEP
Brief summary: Patients with drug-resistant epilepsy may have cardiac dysautonomia, with reduced heart rate variability and increased sympathetic tone. This condition is part of the concept of "epileptic heart" and could be a risk factor for sudden death, one of the main causes of excess mortality in patients with severe epilepsy in adulthood. The mechanism of this cardiac impairment is poorly understood. The hypothalamus, due to its role as the subcortical conductor of the autonomic nervous system and its known links with the limbic system, particularly the amygdala and hippocampus, is a candidate for a key intermediary role in the impact of seizures on cardiorespiratory function. The investigators wish to investigate the hypothesis that cardiac dysautonomia in patients with drug-resistant epilepsy is correlated with structural changes in the hypothalamus. The investigators wish to study in 7Tesla MRI the volume of the different hypothalamic nuclei, the amygdalo- hypothalamic and
chunks.title: Study of the Link Between Structural Alterations in the Hypothalamus and Cardiac Dysautonomia in Drug-resistant Epilepsy

chunks.text: ges in the hypothalamus. The investigators wish to study in 7Tesla MRI the volume of the different hypothalamic nuclei, the amygdalo- hypothalamic and hypothalamo-bulbar connectivity, as well as the metabolic content in spectroscopy in patients with drug-resistant epilepsy, and correlate these data with the sympathetic and parasympathetic tones of these patients.

It is the amount of air expelled after maximum inspiration following a normal breath, expressed in liters. chunks.title: Rehabilitation Through Virtual Immersion & Integrated Exposure for Mild Traumatic Brain Injury (ReVIVE for mTBI)

chunks.text:
Intervention: Virtual Reality (DEVICE). ReVIVE is a virtual reality (VR)-based rehabilitation intervention delivered over six weekly sessions as an adjunct to standard care for individuals with PTSD following mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI). Using an Oculus Quest VR headset, participants complete approximately 10 minutes of acclimation followed by 30 minutes of immersive activities. The intervention incorporates mindfulness, breathing and grounding exercises, emotional regulation, and cognitive and functional activities within simulated everyday environments. Scenarios are designed to support engagement with progressively more complex environments and tasks. Intervention tolerability is monitored using the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire before and after VR sessions. Standard care, including routine psychotherapy and medication management, continues throughout the study.
Intervention: Standard Psychotherapy (BEHAVIORAL). Standard psychotherapy consists of ongoing therapy received by participants before enrollment and continued throughout the study as part of the participants usual care. Sessions focus on identifying emotions, recognizing cognitive shifts and difficulties,
chunks.title: Rehabilitation Through Virtual Immersion & Integrated Exposure for Mild Traumatic Brain Injury (ReVIVE for mTBI)

chunks.text:
ed throughout the study as part of the participants usual care. Sessions focus on identifying emotions, recognizing cognitive shifts and difficulties, supporting real-time emotional and cognitive regulation, and facilitating interpersonal processing and emotional labeling. Psychotherapy frequency and treatment decisions remain at the discretion of participants' treating clinicians and are not standardized or altered by the study. Participants assigned to the control arm continue standard psychotherapy and medication management without receiving the study's virtual reality intervention.
Study arm: ReVIVE Virtual Reality + Standard Care (EXPERIMENTAL). Participants randomized to this arm will receive six weekly sessions of virtual reality (VR)-based rehabilitation in addition to standard care, including routine psychotherapy and medication management. Each session includes approximately 10 minutes of VR acclimation followed by 30 minutes of immersive VR activities designed to support emotional regulation, cognitive functioning, and functional rehabilitation. Activities incorporate mindfulness, breathing and grounding techniques, and everyday environments and tasks, with scenarios
chunks.title: Rehabilitation Through Virtual Immersion & Integrated Exposure for Mild Traumatic Brain Injury (ReVIVE for mTBI)

chunks.text:
functional rehabilitation. Activities incorporate mindfulness, breathing and grounding techniques, and everyday environments and tasks, with scenarios progressing in complexity. Intervention tolerability will be monitored using the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire administered before and after VR sessions.
Study arm: Standard Care Only (ACTIVE_COMPARATOR). Participants randomized to this arm will continue receiving standard care, including routine psychotherapy and medication management, without the addition of virtual reality (VR)-based rehabilitation. Participants will still complete study assessments at the scheduled time points to evaluate changes PTSD-related symptoms over the study period.

chunks.text:
Primary outcome: Change in PTSD Symptom Severity Measured by the Davidson Trauma Scale (DTS)
Time frame: Baseline, midpoint assessment at approximately 3 weeks, final post-intervention assessment approximately 1 week post completion of the six-week intervention.
PTSD-related symptom severity will be assessed using the 17-item Davidson Trauma Scale (DTS), a self-report measure evaluating the frequency and severity of trauma-related symptoms, including intrusion, avoidance, and hyperarousal. Changes in DTS scores will be evaluated over the study period. The DTS yields a frequency score (ranging from 0 to 68), severity score (ranging from 0 to 68), and total score (ranging from 0 to 136). Higher score worse severity/frequency.

Eligibility criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

1. Age 18 years or older.
2. Definite diagnosis of cerebral venous thrombosis confirmed by neuroimaging, including computed tomography venography (CTV), magnetic resonance venography (MRV), or digital subtraction angiography (DSA).
3. Admitted to Danang Hospital for acute or subacute management.
4. Patient or legally authorized representative provides written informed consent to participate in the registry.

Exclusion Criteria:

1. Non-thrombotic occlusion of cerebral veins or sinuses (e.g., direct tumor invasion, vascular malformation, or extrinsic mechanical compression without thrombosis).
2. Pre-existing advanced terminal illness or severe co-morbid condition with a life expectancy of less than 6 months prior to CVT presentation (e.g., end-stage malignancy, advanced organ failure).
3. pre-mRS ≥ 2
4. Inability or refusal of the patient or their legal representative to complete the 6-month follow-up assessment.
5. Refusal to provide informed consent.

Patients receive therapeutic anticoagulation according to standard clinical guidelines (low-molecular-weight heparin or unfractionated heparin in the acute phase, followed by oral anticoagulants including vitamin K antagonists or direct oral anticoagulants), along with supportive medical care and endovascular treatment when indicated.

chunks.text:
Primary outcome: Favorable Functional Outcome Assessed by the Modified Rankin Scale (mRS)
Time frame: At 6 months post-diagnosis
Functional status is evaluated using the modified Rankin Scale (mRS), a standardized clinical tool measuring the degree of disability or dependence in daily activities. The scale ranges from 0 (no symptoms) to 6 (death). A favorable functional outcome is defined as an mRS score of 0 to 1 (complete recovery or no significant disability despite symptoms)

Title: Danang Cerebral Venous Thrombosis Registry
Conditions: Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis, Stroke, Cerebral Venous Thrombosis
Brief summary: Cerebral venous thrombosis (CVT) is an uncommon but potentially life-threatening type of stroke, predominantly affecting young adults and women. Although prompt diagnosis and anticoagulant therapy can lead to favorable outcomes, data regarding the clinical spectrum, neuroimaging patterns, risk factors, and long-term functional recovery of CVT patients in central Vietnam remain limited.

This prospective observational study aims to establish a hospital-based registry to investigate the clinical characteristics, neuroimaging features, etiology, and treatment outcomes of patients diagnosed with cerebral venous thrombosis at Danang Hospital.

All consecutive patients with confirmed CVT admitted to Danang Hospital are enrolled and managed according to standard clinical protocols. Participants are monitored throughout their hospital stay to assess acute manifestations, imaging abnormalities (on CT/CTV or MRI/MRV), and inpatient complications.
